mainText: TradeHQ — Free Paper Trading SimulatorLearning notes: TradeHQ — Free Paper Trading SimulatorPractice simulated trading across 170 assets with $100,000 in virtual cash. No real money is involved. Learn order mechanics, portfolio tracking, and risk concepts across stocks, crypto, ETFs, forex and commodities.Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.What TradeHQ actually isTradeHQ is a free paper-trading simulator for people learning how markets work. Every account starts with $100,000 in virtual cash. Nothing on the site touches real money: there is no brokerage account, no deposit, no withdrawal and no order ever reaches an exchange. Supported holdings use periodically refreshed provider quotes. Unsupported assets can use fixed simulator prices, and charts may show synthetic practice candles. Price and chart labels explain their source and freshness.A practice account lets you examine decisions without putting savings at risk. For example, compare how different quantities change a hypothetical loss, or record why you changed an exit plan. These exercises do not establish why most beginners lose money or guarantee that practice changes later behaviour.What you can do herePaper trade 170 instruments across stocks, crypto, ETFs, forex and commodities using market orders.Track a full practice portfolio — open positions, realised and unrealised P&L, maximum drawdown, open-position P&L dispersion and allocation snapshots.Explore four bundled course tracks (options, futures, macroeconomics and decision behaviour) and additional approved catalog releases, with quizzes and completion badges.Read a 49-term trading glossary written in plain language, each entry with a detailed explanation and a worked example.Follow step-by-step guides for individual assets, side-by-side asset comparisons, and named strategy walkthroughs.Keep a trading journal, build daily streaks with the daily challenge, and run a 30-day practice duel against a friend.Who it is for, and who it is not forTradeHQ is built for beginners and self-directed learners who want a place to rehearse market mechanics and a repeatable process without using real money. It can also be useful in classroom or independent-study settings.It is not for you if you want signals, copy-trading, portfolio management, or someone to tell you what to buy. We do not publish price targets, we do not run a Discord with calls, and we do not accept payment for coverage of any asset. If you are looking for a recommendation, this is the wrong site.Ways to begin learningOpen the markets page and pick one instrument you already recognise.Read its available educational notes and distinguish identified facts from hypotheses about price changes.Compare fictional quantities and price changes to understand their effect on a virtual account.Record the assumptions and limitations of the selected worksheet.Review what the example illustrates at a time that suits your schedule; no transaction is required.What educational simulation can and cannot showFictional examples can explain market mechanics without requiring a real transaction. Practice does not guarantee profit or replace independent education. A beginner can practice buying and selling holdings with virtual capital, then review those decisions without risking savings. TradeHQ currently supports market orders only; it does not simulate resting limit orders or short positions.A simulator does not reproduce the financial or personal consequences of a real loss. A written record can support review, but no pattern of participation establishes the quality of future decisions.Common questionsIs TradeHQ free? Yes, entirely. There is no paid tier, no trial and no card required.Do I need an account? No. Practice trading, courses and the glossary work without signing up. An optional account supports profiles and community features. Account cash, positions and server-recorded trades restore across devices when available; earlier guest trade history and journals remain on the original browser, while signed-in lessons and journey progress can sync privately when online.Is the money real? No. Every balance, order and result is simulated, and the platform holds no funds.Are the prices real? Supported assets use periodically refreshed provider observations. Unsupported assets can use fixed simulator prices; charts may be synthetic. Check each source and timestamp rather than assuming a continuous exchange feed.Does TradeHQ execute investments or provide personalized advice? No. Trading examples and educational indicator labels are illustrative, not personal recommendations, and the simulator places virtual orders only.Where is my data? Guest practice records stay in your browser. Signed-in cash, positions and server-recorded trades are stored in Supabase and restored when the service is available. Guest trade history, journal entries and streaks remain browser-held; signed-in lessons and journey progress can sync privately. A badge count alone is not the complete course record.References and related pagesBrowse all marketsStructured trading coursesBeginner practice guideTrading glossaryAsset-by-asset guidesAbout TradeHQEducational simulation only — not financial advice. Virtual money; no brokerage transactions. Quotes may be delayed, cached, unavailable or fixed simulator values; generated charts are labelled separately. Practice results do not predict investment outcomes.

Paper Trade 170 AssetsLearning notes: Paper Trade 170 AssetsChoose from 170 simulated assets and practise placing buy or sell orders. Every account starts with $100,000 in virtual cash. Educational simulation — no real money and no brokerage relationship.Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.How the practice trading desk worksChoose an instrument, side and quantity to preview a market practice order. Guest orders use the browser's virtual execution input and are recorded in that browser. For signed-in orders, the server selects an eligible quote at execution, so the fill price may differ from the estimate. Account cash, positions and server-recorded trade history restore across devices when the service is available.The desk supports market practice orders only. A signed-in order may pause if an eligible quote is unavailable. The glossary explains limit and stop orders. Learners choose their own quantities and compare hypothetical exposure to practise the arithmetic. The simplified fill model does not validate real-market risk management.What to practise on the deskPosition sizing: compare hypothetical quantities under the same adverse price move. A fixed fraction does not guarantee a smoother equity curve, and the current simulator does not execute automatic stop orders.Exit assumptions: compare the stated hypothetical price with alternative observations; an assumption is not a resting order.Entry timing: note the price you intended versus the price you received on a fast-moving instrument, and record the gap in the journal.Concentration: compare otherwise identical hypothetical portfolios with different holdings and state the assumptions.Limits of any simulatorTradeHQ applies a fixed 0.1% virtual fee to each simulated buy or sell, but that classroom input is not a real broker's fee schedule. Simplified practice fills do not reproduce real-world spreads, slippage, overnight financing or taxes; practice also lacks the emotional weight of risking your own money. Treat results as evidence about your practice process, not a forecast of live returns. Past simulated performance does not predict future real-world performance.Orders supported by this simulatorThe market practice order shows a price estimate. Signed-in fills use an eligible quote at execution. Real market orders seek execution at available prices and may fill at different prices or not complete during market interruptions.Limit orders appear in the learning material. The current simulator supports market practice orders only.Closing a position: sell some or all of an existing holding. You cannot sell more than you hold or open a short position. Completed buys and sells appear in portfolio trade history.Optional review of fictional examplesChoose an exercise with a stated question, record the assumptions before placing orders and review the result afterwards. Transaction count alone does not measure learning or validate a strategy.A sample journal can ask whether the observed virtual quantity matched the written assumption, what changed after the quoted timestamp and which execution costs are missing. A journal helps review choices but does not establish improved returns.References and related pagesChoose an instrumentYour practice portfolioHow-to guides per assetStrategy walkthroughsEducational simulation only — not financial advice. Markets OverviewLearning notes: Markets OverviewBrowse 170 simulated markets across major asset classes. Explore movers, sentiment-style indicators and sector groupings, then practise with $100,000 virtual cash. This page uses generated display data for education, not live market observations.Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.What is on the markets pageThe markets page lists every instrument available in the simulator, grouped by asset class: US equities, cryptocurrencies, exchange-traded funds, major and minor forex pairs, and commodities. Each row shows a generated practice price and practice change, and links to a dedicated page for that instrument. Changes are seeded initially and then describe the latest generated update, not a measured daily return.The Markets page uses simulated practice prices and estimated changes for visual feedback. Provider-backed, delayed or cached data may appear elsewhere on TradeHQ and is labelled separately when available. This is a learning environment, not a market-data terminal — do not use these quotes for any real decision.How to choose what to practise firstStart with something you already understand as a customer or user — a retailer, an index ETF, or a currency you have actually spent.The generated list cannot measure actual liquidity or spreads; study those concepts separately using dated reference material.Choose a manageable set of instruments and record what each exercise tests. No fixed study period establishes competence.Use the linked educational notes to distinguish an instrument's definition from uncertain explanations of price changes.Asset classes explained brieflyStocks: fractional ownership of a listed company; move on earnings, guidance, sector rotation and rates.ETFs: funds with stated holdings and objectives. Diversification, concentration, leverage and product structure affect risk.Crypto: digital assets traded on venues with varying operating schedules, liquidity and risks. No fixed volatility or price relationship is implied.Forex: relative pricing of two currencies; central-bank announcements, economic data and other conditions are possible research topics.Commodities: exposures linked to physical goods, supply, demand and seasonal conditions. Company earnings and equity prices can also have seasonal influences.Reading a market list without being misledA percentage move needs a clearly stated interval, observation source and comparison sample. A 3% move can have different meanings for different instruments and periods; it is not a permanent volatility category. Generated practice changes do not establish a real-market daily range.Volume describes trading activity when it is supplied by a valid market-data source. It does not establish the identity or intentions of buyers and sellers, or prove that a price move will continue or reverse. Simulated or unavailable volume cannot confirm an actual market event.Things that trip beginners on a markets screenAssuming a large recent gain predicts the next price move; an observed change does not determine future returns or a suitable entry.Assuming a low nominal price alone establishes whether an asset is inexpensive; the units and method of valuation matter.Treating any ETF as automatically low-risk: sector funds and concentrated funds still carry market and holding-specific risks.Ignoring market hours: equities gap overnight, crypto trades continuously, forex has session-driven liquidity.References and related pagesOpen the trading deskGlossary of market termsStructured coursesAsset comparisonsEducational simulation only — not financial advice. Practice PortfolioLearning notes: Practice PortfolioReview simulated positions, trades, P&L, drawdown and allocation snapshots. Guest records stay in your browser; account cash, positions and server-recorded trades restore when the service is available. Server-recorded account trades restore across devices; earlier guest history and journals remain browser-held.Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.What the practice portfolio tracksThe portfolio page shows open positions with entry prices, current practice prices and unrealised profit or loss, plus eligible recorded transaction history. Guest records live in local storage. Signed-in cash, positions and server-recorded transactions can restore when the service is available; clearing browser data does not delete that account copy. Earlier guest records and journals remain browser-held.Beyond raw P&L, the page calculates fee-inclusive closed-result win rate, average win versus average loss, current open-position return dispersion, and practice maximum drawdown. These summarize recorded outcomes and exposures that can help you review your practice process. The chart can include generated history; it is not a verified sequence of account observations.How to read your own numbers honestlyCompare win rate, average realized win, average realized loss and costs together. A high win rate alone does not establish a positive result.Maximum drawdown describes a selected peak-to-trough decline. It does not measure every risk or predict your response to a real loss.A short run is an observation, not proof of a repeatable advantage. Selection, dependence, costs and changing conditions matter; no fixed trade count establishes an edge.If one position contributes most of a measured result, that observation alone cannot establish the effect of a method.Why results here do not transfer one-to-oneThe simulator applies a 0.1% practice transaction fee, rather than a real broker fee schedule. It does not model financing costs, taxes or actual market execution. Review practice results alongside these limits; they do not predict real-money results.The metrics explained in plain languageUnrealised P&L: the difference between an open position's current marked value and its cost basis. Closing a position records realised P&L using its actual recorded proceeds and cost basis, which can differ from the earlier mark. All balances and results here remain virtual.Realised P&L: the result of trades you have actually closed. It is an accounting result, not a measure of decision quality.Open positions in profit: the share of current open positions showing positive unrealised P&L. This is not a closed-trade win rate.Open-position P&L dispersion: the spread of current position returns around their average. This is a snapshot, not a Sharpe ratio or time-series volatility measure.Practice maximum drawdown: the largest fall from a peak in locally stored snapshots, which can include generated hourly backfill. It is not an observed market record or proof that a strategy is survivable.Reviewing the portfolio weeklyChoose a repeatable review interval for virtual results and compare the information recorded before each order with what became known later. A loss alone cannot establish whether the original reasoning was sound.Compare the largest virtual gain with its position size, price change, quotation source and costs. A large one-off outcome does not by itself establish skill or predict a similar future result.References and related pagesPlace a practice tradeRisk management guideWhat drawdown meansEducational simulation only — not financial advice. Your First Virtual Trade, ExplainedLearning notes: Your First Virtual Trade, ExplainedTry an optional Daily Practice scenario, then follow five guided steps to understand an order, place a voluntary simulated trade, review cash and holdings, reflect, and choose what to learn next. No account or real money is required.Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.Step 1 — Understand an order before placing oneThe optional Daily Practice scenario comes first. In the guided lesson that follows, compare a displayed quote with the execution price. Consider two fictional shares showing $50 each. Their quoted purchase value is $100, and a 0.1% simulated fee adds $0.10. The estimated debit is therefore $100.10, assuming a $50 fill. The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission's Investor.gov guidance explains that a real market order's execution price is not guaranteed by the last quote. The simulator is simpler, and must not be mistaken for a live brokerage.The learner answers a short understanding check before entering the trading desk. The exercise presents an invented scenario for reading costs and uncertainty, not a stock recommendation or a return promise.Steps 2 and 3 — Place a voluntary virtual trade, then inspect the numbersBefore opening the main virtual trading terminal, learners can optionally try a five-round fictional Practice Arena warm-up covering cash, holdings and a model fee. The warm-up's invented prices and browser-local balances are separate from the $100,000 trading portfolio, do not enter leaderboards, and do not advance the five-step journey. It can be skipped at any time; an Arena completion is not a saved guided trade.The guided link opens the normal virtual trading terminal, optionally selecting an illustrative asset. It never places an order on the learner's behalf. The visitor chooses a quantity and explicitly confirms any simulated transaction. A successful saved trade advances the journey; merely pressing a guide button does not.The next stage reads the learner's actual saved practice data. It shows remaining virtual cash, total account value, number of holdings, and the chosen trade's quantity, execution price, calculated fee and cash movement. Open-position returns change with the available reference price and are not guaranteed cash profits. A refreshed or delayed quote can differ from an earlier reference.Steps 4 and 5 — Reflect and return for daily practiceLearners write a private reflection explaining what surprised them about the price or fee and what they will check before another exercise. New reflection text stays in the browser even when signed in. Only the completed step can sync with the account. Older reflections that already synced remain private. TradeHQ then recommends a risk-management lesson and the existing Daily Practice exercises; completion does not certify readiness to risk real money.The journey records completed steps in browser storage so guest visitors can return later on the same browser. Signed-in members can also privately sync supported lessons, quiz drafts, reading position and journey progress between devices when online. A course's most-recent-lesson record helps resume the right lesson. Clearing guest browser data can remove that guest's progress; portfolio backups do not include learning records.What a first practice result can and cannot showA fictional profit or loss is useful for checking arithmetic, exposure, and whether the learner understood their own decision. It does not reproduce real transaction liquidity, bid/ask spreads, slippage, tax obligations or the consequences of risking money. A short winning streak is not evidence of an investing skill. The intended result of this lesson is a better explanation of the order and its limitations, not a trade signal.References and related pagesOptional fictional decision warm-up before the first virtual tradeVoluntary virtual trading terminalInspect your simulated portfolio and fee recordsDaily Practice exercisesResume a structured courseRisk-management lessonSEC Investor.gov: Types of OrdersEducational simulation only — not financial advice. Learn to TradeLearning notes: Learn to TradeStructured lessons, a 49-term glossary, and long-form guides on stocks, crypto, ETFs and technical analysis. Supported spot mechanics can be explored in the simulator; derivatives and unsupported indicators use separate conceptual worksheets.Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.Two different ways to learn hereTradeHQ separates learning into two formats on purpose. Full courses organize related topics into multi-lesson tracks with quizzes, source notes and completion badges. Quick reads address narrower questions. Neither format certifies complete mastery.Both formats link to the virtual practice desk. Reading explains concepts; a simulated order can illustrate the arithmetic and interface, but the resulting virtual performance cannot validate financial competence.A suggested order for complete beginnersUse the beginner practice guide to learn what virtual orders, prices and fees mean, then follow a structured course for more detail.Use the trading psychology course to examine records, decisions and bias; it does not assign a universal cause to beginner losses.Use the macro course to read releases and distinguish observed information from uncertain explanations of price changes.Study the options and futures lessons as conceptual examples of contracts, leverage and risk; TradeHQ does not execute real or simulated derivative contracts.Keep the glossary open in a second tab and look up every unfamiliar term as it appears.How this material is written and reviewedLessons are designed for independent study. Relevant sources accompany many definitions and examples, while some references are background rather than evidence of a strategy's effectiveness. Numerical scenarios are illustrative, not forecasts or individual financial recommendations. Report missing or misleading citations through the Contact page.What a realistic learning timeline looks likeLearning timelines differ with prior knowledge, study time and the task being practised. A calendar duration does not establish proficiency or investment readiness. Set an observable learning goal, such as explaining an order fill or reproducing a fee calculation, and record which parts remain uncertain.For a concrete self-check, write down a quote price, quantity and the simulator's 0.1% fee, calculate the virtual purchase cost, then compare your result with the practice order panel. If the figures differ, inspect quantity, rounding and quote freshness before moving on. Completing this exercise checks one skill, not overall investing readiness.How to tell good trading education from badGood material explains mechanics and probability; bad material promises returns.Good material shows losing examples; bad material only shows winners.Check whether a source actually supports the claim. A primary document can provide useful evidence; a screenshot without verifiable context is insufficient on its own.Good material tells you who it is not for; bad material claims to suit everyone.A credible educational source separates observations from forecasts, documents data limitations and does not use time pressure as evidence.References and related pagesStructured coursesBeginner practice guideTrading glossaryCountry guidesEducational simulation only — not financial advice. Beginner Trading Practice GuideLearning notes: Beginner Trading Practice GuideAn introduction to the virtual practice dashboard, order mechanics and a worked buy/sell-fee example. Links to longer courses and reference material; $100,000 is simulated money, not an investment account.Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.What this page actually providesThis page is a starting map and interactive practice dashboard, not a complete textbook or independently tested trading course. It introduces quote reading, simulated market orders, fees and reviewing hypothetical outcomes. Use the linked structured courses for deeper explanations of instruments, order types and portfolio concepts. The exercises illustrate arithmetic and questions to ask, not a profitable strategy.Four checks for a virtual practice exerciseExposure: quantify the share of virtual cash used and calculate what a chosen adverse price change would do to the holding.Exit assumptions: write down both a higher and a lower hypothetical sale price. TradeHQ does not support resting limit or stop orders.Observation quality: record the quote source, timestamp, asset and quote currency. A generated chart need not reproduce traded market history.Review: retain the original assumptions, both virtual fees and alternative outcomes. One or ten practice results do not establish a repeatable advantage.Worked example: virtual shares, fees and two outcomesAssume a purely hypothetical purchase of ten shares at $50 each. The gross cost is $500 and a 0.1% virtual purchase fee is $0.50, so the total cash used is $500.50. If the assumed sale price is $46, the gross proceeds are $460 and a 0.1% virtual sale fee is $0.46; net proceeds are $459.54. Compared with the original $500.50 cost, the round trip produces a loss of $40.96.For the same ten shares, a separate hypothetical sale at $54 yields $540 gross, less a $0.54 virtual sale fee, or $539.46 net. Subtract the $500.50 initial cost to get a gain of $38.96. These prices are invented, not a forecast or observed fills. Actual transactions can involve spreads, slippage, taxes and other costs not captured here.What this simulator cannot teach by itselfTradeHQ offers virtual market orders, not real brokerage transactions, short positions or resting limit/stop orders. Even when a displayed quote comes from an external provider, a simulated fill does not establish that the same price or liquidity would be available on an exchange.Use the structured courses and linked sources to check concepts rather than treating a synthetic sentiment label, an indicator, or a hypothetical growth calculator as a verified trading signal. Practice outcomes do not predict real-money results.The vocabulary you need before anything elseBid and ask: at a given time, the best displayed bid and ask are quoted buying and selling prices. Their difference is the spread. Actual fills and costs can differ from that snapshot.Liquidity: the availability of buyers and sellers at prices and quantities. Limited liquidity can make a real order harder or more costly to execute.Volatility: a measure of price variation over a stated period. It describes past movement; it cannot dictate one universally appropriate exit level or position size.Leverage: exposure larger than posted funds through borrowing or derivatives. Gains and losses can be magnified, and collateral or liquidation rules vary by product and venue. TradeHQ does not provide leverage.Expectancy example, not a forecast: five hypothetical wins of $30 and five losses of $20 total $50 before costs. Ten $2 round-trip fees reduce that to $30 net. This invented ten-trade record is too small and artificial to establish a repeatable advantage.A first-month planWeek one: label the bid, ask, spread and quote time on an example, then inspect virtual market orders without using real funds.Week two: write assumptions before a virtual example, including quantity, fee, possible lower sale price and an alternative outcome.Week three: check each recorded virtual outcome against its original assumptions; distinguish a mark from an executable real-world quote.Week four: compare the journal entries for missing costs, changed assumptions and hindsight bias. Note what the simulation cannot test.References and related pagesStructured courses and quizzesGlossary: order terms and market mechanicsStrategy concepts and limitsVirtual practice deskEducational simulation only — not financial advice. mainText: Trading Mentor — Curated KnowledgeLearning notes: Trading Mentor — Curated KnowledgeAsk the mentor about trading concepts. This chat uses a built-in answer library and local topic matching, with no AI API request. Answers can miss your question and are educational only. Practice what you learn on the free simulator with $100,000 virtual cash.Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.What the rule-based mentor doesThis chat matches your question to a built-in library of educational answers about trading concepts, indicators and order types. It does not call a language model, read your journal or assess a proposed investment. Separate portfolio mentor tools can use the simulated figures shown on that page.What it will not doIt does not give buy or sell recommendations, price targets or personalised financial advice.It does not know your real financial circumstances and cannot assess suitability.Authored answers and topic matching can be wrong or miss the question. Check important claims against a primary source.It is not a substitute for a licensed professional in your own jurisdiction.Getting useful answersAsk about mechanics rather than what to buy. Try a supported topic such as risk/reward, diversification or dollar-cost averaging. Topic matching may return a general answer or miss your intent; it does not provide a personalised suitability assessment. Derivatives lessons are conceptual because this simulator does not trade options or futures contracts.Good questions to ask itExplain what happens to a call option's value if the stock does not move for two weeks.What is the difference between a stop-loss order and a stop-limit order, and when does each fail?My practice win rate is 60% but I am down overall — what does that imply about my exits?Why do forex pairs move on interest-rate announcements?Explain the distinction between a fictional holding's marked value and the total account value.How it works and what it costsThe mentor uses a built-in library of authored educational answers, topic matching and calculations. Chat does not call an AI provider or use AI credits. Its coverage is limited to the available topics; an unfamiliar question may receive a general explanation rather than a tailored answer.Mentor topic matching happens in your browser and does not send the conversation to an AI provider. Advertising and analytics are separate services described in the privacy policy. Educational answers can still contain mistakes or omit context; check substantive claims against a primary source before relying on them.A reminder about limitsNo assistant, however fluent, can assess whether a trade suits your finances, and none of the answers here are regulated advice. Treat the mentor as a patient tutor for mechanics and vocabulary, and take anything that sounds like a recommendation as a sign the question needs rewording.References and related pagesStructured coursesGlossaryBeginner guideEducational simulation only — not financial advice. Daily Trading ChallengeLearning notes: Daily Trading ChallengePractise a quick scenario or go deeper with a hypothetical case, labelled visual, 10 linked questions and worked explanations. 50 exercises rotate; new banks are targeted every two months and require owner approval. Answers stay on this browser.Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.How the daily challenge worksDaily offers a quick hypothetical market scenario alongside a longer ten-question case study. You choose a response, compare the reasoning and trade-offs, then answer a short bonus knowledge question about market basics. Completing the quick reasoning step or all ten case-study questions advances the browser-stored streak at most once per local day. Directional reflections are not forecast scores.The scenario's prices, news events and dates are exercise inputs, not a report of what happened in today's markets. Choosing long, short or hold records a reflection; it does not place an order. Use the explanation to compare assumptions and uncertainty rather than treating completion as evidence of forecasting skill.Using a daily habit to support reviewReview the reasoning and arithmetic when it is useful; no particular frequency establishes skill.A short exercise is optional. Choose a study interval that fits your schedule.A streak counts participation; it does not establish that a particular study habit has formed.After a missed day, resume when your schedule allows; a streak is a participation aid, not a skill grade.A longer daily practice sessionThe deeper exercise develops one case across ten linked questions, so the learner can calculate an input, interpret the result and identify a limitation. Topics rotate between portfolio arithmetic, transaction costs and supported orders, price-data freshness, risk and uncertainty, and decision habits. The visuals show selected hypothetical inputs with numeric labels; they are not live market charts. Worked explanations appear after each submitted answer, including when the answer was wrong.After you finish, the case takeaway provides a review guide for checking the reasoning. Checked answers are saved on this browser. After the first saved answer, the case keeps its own snapshot if a new bank is approved while you are working. Clearing site data removes this local history; an account does not synchronize this case history to another device.The configured generation workflow targets a new 50-exercise bank every two calendar months in five parts using the configured Gemini API. A target schedule is not a publication guarantee. Each completed bank remains private and editable in the owner’s admin panel until final review and approval. If generation hits a quota limit, fails validation or awaits review, the approved bank continues rotating. Fifty exercises can therefore repeat before the next bank begins; revisits are review practice rather than a claim of brand-new daily content. The feature does not use a paid provider fallback.What the challenges coverA hypothetical market scenario with stated exercise inputs, rather than current market news.Comparing long, short and hold reasoning without grading one market direction as objectively correct.A bank of 50 deeper exercises, each with a substantial hypothetical case, a labelled visual and ten linked questions with worked explanations.The existing short bonus quiz plus a case takeaway with a review guide.How the streak is countedA streak advances once per calendar day in your own local time zone, so completing a challenge late one evening and early the next morning still counts as two consecutive days. The counter lives in your browser, which means clearing site data resets it and using a different device starts a separate count even when you have an account; sign-in does not back up local streaks.There is no penalty for missing a day beyond the counter resetting, and longer streaks unlock browser-local completion badges, not prizes or qualifications. Nothing about the challenge involves money, prizes or entry fees.If you miss a dayNothing bad happens beyond the counter going back to one. The purpose of the streak is to make practice frequent, not to punish a missed evening, and restarting after a gap is the normal experience rather than a failure. The counter is not a judgment about you or a measurement of future returns.If daily practice does not fit your schedule, choose a workable review rhythm. A record of what you learned is more informative than a raw session count.References and related pagesPractice deskGlossaryChallenge a friendEducational simulation only — not financial advice. TradeHQ Practice ArenaLearning notes: TradeHQ Practice ArenaPractice Arena is a free, self-contained interactive training exercise. Choose a beginner or intermediate scenario, observe deliberately fictional prices, and decide whether to buy a small exercise position, sell already held units or wait. Each decision reveals another invented observation and explains the accounting and assumptions. The Arena begins with its own $10,000 fictional cash ledger. The model charges a 0.1% fee on virtual buys and sells, and records exercise choices privately in this browser. It never places an order on TradeHQ's normal virtual trading terminal, changes a user portfolio, alters a public leaderboard, or consults a real-market quote. A favorable exercise result cannot establish trading competence or forecast real performance. After reviewing a scenario, continue with the beginner journey, risk lesson or deeper Daily Practice.Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.How Practice Arena worksPractice Arena is an interactive training exercise built around deliberate choices rather than trading predictions. Choose one of three authored paths: Your First Decision, Size Changes Everything, or Stay With the Plan. Each path contains five small decision rounds. The next hypothetical observation is hidden until you choose to buy a fictional unit, sell units you already hold, or wait without making an order. This helps you practise noticing assumptions without claiming that a particular price direction is objectively correct.All instruments and prices in the Arena are invented classroom examples. They are not historical exchange observations, live quotes, market forecasts or recommendations to buy or sell any real security. A user can enter the exercise without an account, paying a fee or connecting a brokerage. The separate practice balance begins with 10,000 fictional dollars for the purposes of these specific decisions. This is not the main TradeHQ simulator's 100,000-dollar balance, and nothing in the Arena sends an order to the main trading terminal.A worked illustration of the virtual ledgerImagine a fictional asset displayed at $100 a unit, an exercise cash balance of $10,000 and an order to purchase one unit. The classroom calculation uses the purchase notional of $100 plus a 0.1% transaction fee of $0.10. Exercise cash becomes $9,899.90 and the held unit is initially worth $100 at the same fictional mark, leaving marked equity of $9,999.90. The decrease is the modelled fee, not the loss of the entire purchase value.If the next invented observation is $102, the one held unit is marked at $102 and the combined exercise equity would be $10,001.90. If a user simply observes instead of buying, no units are purchased or sold, cash stays unchanged and no transaction fee is charged. A sale is allowed only for units actually held; a user cannot open a short position in this teaching exercise. Costs and changes are displayed immediately after each decision. These examples describe arithmetic, not actual exchange settlement, liquidity, taxes or execution.Why the Arena asks for a reasonBefore revealing the next scenario observation, you may write what you are trying to test or why you would prefer to observe without placing an order. Afterward, the review panel compares the recorded action with the next invented mark, the modelled fee, remaining cash and the value of any held units. A profitable fictional decision is not declared a good decision, and an unprofitable one is not automatically described as a mistake. The purpose is to examine what is known, what was assumed and how the decision affects the ledger.The first path focuses on basic cash and fee accounting, the second on the dollar effect of position quantity, and the intermediate path on distinguishing evidence from unsupported claims under changing conditions. The next step can be an existing beginner journey, a risk-management lesson or a deeper Daily Practice case. The three paths are finite and can be repeated; TradeHQ does not advertise unlimited new historical market scenarios.After completing five rounds, the review separates the value effect of fictional price changes from the virtual fees charged for buying or selling. The price effect includes changes in units still held, so it is not necessarily a realized trading result. Learners can expand a chronological record of every decision and its optional stated reason, then write a private closing reflection about what to test again. This information remains on their device.The optional usefulness prompt lets a learner choose whether an exercise was useful, confusing or too easy. Choosing an option does not transmit it. If a learner explicitly opens the Contact page, TradeHQ can prefill an email draft that they may edit and decide whether to send. Selecting a usefulness response does not automatically submit the response. Separate performance and optional analytics requests are described in the Privacy Policy.Privacy, limitations and what the result meansArena exercises use intentionally fictional prices and an isolated local ledger. They never change the signed-in practice portfolio, guest simulator balance, public rankings or verified competition records.Decisions, optional notes and completion history stay in the same browser. Clearing site data may erase them, and signing in does not currently synchronize Arena sessions across devices.The exercise does not simulate market spreads, order-book depth, slippage, broker regulation, borrowing, stop execution, tax costs or the emotional consequences of risking real savings.A finished session is a record of educational participation, not investment advice, a skill certification, a personalized trading recommendation or evidence of likely real financial returns.Visitors can leave without making a trade. Waiting is a deliberate choice and carries no fictional transaction fee.Optional Arena usage milestones use Amplitude only after an adult visitor confirms they are at least 18 and explicitly accepts the renewed analytics choice; no prior acceptance is reused. Replay and automatic interactions are disabled in the website analytics setup. These events can indicate a start, completion, resume or later same-browser visit, but do not transmit decisions, balances, portfolio identities or written reflections. Rejecting analytics does not disable the simulator. A five-minute voluntary study offers before-and-after concept questions and optional feedback; the answers stay in the current page until the participant explicitly copies or prepares an email, and no message is sent automatically.References and related pagesFirst virtual trade journeyDaily practice with worked answersRisk-management lessonStructured trading coursesBrowser storage and privacy choicesEducational simulation only — not financial advice. mainText: Privacy PolicyLearning notes: Privacy PolicyGuest simulator records stay in your browser. Account cash, positions and server-recorded trades are stored with Supabase; account, community and consented analytics features also involve provider processing. See the full policy for details.Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.Policy updateLast Updated: November 22, 2026Information TradeHQ HandlesTradeHQ can be used without creating an account. The data handled depends on the features you choose.• Guest simulator data: practice cash, positions and trade history are stored in your browser with a separate browser-local recovery copy. You can download or explicitly restore a portable practice backup JSON file containing trading history and any private journal notes. The backup feature does not upload this file. Backup formats can be manually edited: TradeHQ validates file structure and arithmetic but does not certify authenticity, investment performance or leaderboard ranking. An imported guest file remains unverified. Guest learning-journey progress, course progress, streaks and related settings remain browser-stored. For signed-in users, lesson completion, unfinished quiz answers, reading position and first-trade journey progress may also be saved privately in Supabase and synchronized across devices when online. New beginner-journey reflection text stays on the device. Older reflections already synchronized remain private in the account. Streaks and unrelated browser preferences are not part of this account sync. • Signed-in portfolio data: Supabase stores account cash, positions and server-recorded practice orders, including asset, quantity, execution price, fees, time and simulated result. These account records restore across devices when the service is available. Signed-in users can also download a server-signed current-cycle historical practice export and verify its integrity against their authenticated account. This file may contain account identifiers and private transaction details; it is not publicly shared or accepted as an upload that replaces ranked trades. A first-time browser import stores cash and positions as an unranked portfolio; earlier guest trade history stays in its original browser. Starting a fresh ranked practice cycle archives the previous account snapshot privately. Journals remain browser-held; signed-in lesson and beginner-journey progress can sync privately and are not used to determine public trading ranks. • Optional account data: if you create an account, Supabase processes authentication data such as your email or provider identity and can store profile fields including username, country and bio. • Foundations assessments and certificates: when a signed-in learner uses the optional Foundations programme, Supabase stores account-linked assessment identifiers, scores, possible points and qualifying learning dates. When a learner requests a certificate, TradeHQ stores the recipient name they provide, the programme and milestone, template version, issue date and qualifying assessment evidence so the same certificate can be retrieved. Name corrections are retained as revision history; an earlier name is not erased simply by correcting it. Optional verification sharing stores a hash of the verification credential and its name revision. A person given a valid verification link can check the programme version, milestone and issue date, not the recipient name or private scores. The learner can withdraw or replace the verification link; correcting the name invalidates the previous link. Account deletion cascades to these account-linked Foundations records. A downloaded PDF or copy shared outside TradeHQ is not removed by withdrawing verification or deleting an account. • Community data: signed-in features can store selected practice statistics, public-profile settings, reviews and duel/challenge records. A separate setting, OFF by default, lets a member voluntarily disclose up to 20 current-cycle server-recorded simulated trade entries on an otherwise public profile: asset, buy/sell, quantity, execution price, fee and date. The public data response also includes trade total, simulated realised profit/loss where recorded, and price-source information, even when a visible profile row shows fewer fields. Private journals, reflections, past cycles and browser-only records are never shared by this feature. These are simulated results, not brokerage statements or verified real-money performance. Creating or joining a practice duel requires public profiles. Eligible public duel responses include participant identifiers, invite code, recorded starting values, score values and relevant dates; other visitors may read them while the applicable profiles are public. Switching a profile to private restricts new non-participant access under the duel access policy; participants can retain access, and previously viewed copies cannot be recalled. • Review submissions and interactions: TradeHQ stores your submitted display name (if provided), review text, rating, moderation status and an IP-derived hash used for duplicate prevention. The hash is restricted to authorized backend processing; it is not a public review field. A hash is not necessarily anonymous information. Likes are stored with your account ID and the review ID to enforce one like per account. Public pages show totals, not individual liker identities. Owner replies are public. Reviews removed from public view remain in the private admin panel for restoration. Contact TradeHQ for privacy or removal requests. • Optional TradeHQ Newsletter: if you explicitly request the educational newsletter, TradeHQ stores your email address, consent/confirmation status, the date and source of signup, unsubscribe status, and delivery receipts in private Supabase records. Resend handles email delivery and receives your address for confirmations and issues. We never add prior contact records to the mailing list without permission. Every newsletter provides an unsubscribe link, and you may use the contact page to request deletion. • Contact messages: by default the contact page opens your email app or lets you copy a draft into webmail. If the optional direct-send service is configured, Cloudflare Turnstile processes challenge and connection information and Resend processes the message, sender reply address and recipient information to deliver it to the maintainer's inbox. TradeHQ does not retain direct-send message bodies in its application database. The maintainer's email provider retains delivered messages according to its settings. • Technical data: hosting, authentication, security and abuse-prevention services can receive normal request information such as IP address, browser/device information and server logs. • Website performance: current pages load Cloudflare Web Analytics to measure page loading and performance. Its browser beacon can send the page URL, a page-load identifier, timing and browser performance measurements to Cloudflare, separately from optional Amplitude events. These performance requests can run before an analytics choice and after Amplitude is rejected. Cloudflare states that its Web Analytics usage metrics do not use cookies, local storage or fingerprinting to track individuals. This does not mean that network requests contain no connection information or that every jurisdiction exempts this processing from privacy requirements. • Font delivery: pages request stylesheets and font files from Google Fonts. Google receives the connecting IP address, the requested resource URL and request headers, which can include browser/operating-system information and the referring page according to browser settings. These requests are separate from Amplitude consent and may occur before a choice or after rejection. Google states that its Fonts API does not set or log cookies and does not use Fonts information to create end-user profiles or for targeted advertising. • Optional analytics and advertising data: TradeHQ offers a newly scoped analytics choice only to visitors affirmatively confirming they are at least 18. This confirmation is for optional analytics; it is not an age restriction on lessons, guest practice or sign-in. Visitors under 18 should reject optional analytics. If accepted, Amplitude can receive limited Practice Arena milestone events and two leaderboard registration-flow events (an eligible signed-out leaderboard visit, and a newly created account subsequently authenticated in that same browser within seven days), along with its pseudonymous browser identity and ordinary network metadata. The two leaderboard custom events contain no email, account ID, username, profile details, portfolio data, transaction information, or form content. The temporary seven-day same-browser attribution marker stores only a visit timestamp and is cleared on consent rejection or successful attribution. No custom Amplitude events are sent when optional analytics is declined; the website does not claim visitor identity is anonymous. Amplitude's automatic page, click, form, network and attribution collection and session replay are disabled; the two explicitly triggered attribution events are the only leaderboard funnel measurement. Earlier v1/v2 analytics permissions are not reused. Google AdSense has separate advertising choices and may use cookies or similar identifiers for ad delivery, measurement and, where applicable, personalisation. • Practice Arena research: exercise decisions, private written reasons, closing reflections and history stay in your browser and are not automatically submitted to a research database. An optional, adult-only research questionnaire keeps answers on the open page and only prepares an email if you deliberately choose to do so; you must send that email yourself. Sending an email reveals your sender address and may include other email-provider metadata. Answers are not anonymous once linked with a sender or identifying comments. If you accept Amplitude analytics, TradeHQ may record Arena view/start/finish/resume milestones, scenario ID and difficulty, and whether this browser returned on a later day. Custom Arena events do not include trading choices, portfolio values, account IDs, written notes or questionnaire answers. This opt-in measurement uses the existing Amplitude service's consented visitor identity; it does not create a separate TradeHQ research identifier. Declining analytics disables those custom milestones. A same-browser return event does not prove a person learned or voluntarily returned.TradeHQ does not require a payment card, bank account or brokerage account to place simulated trades.How Information Is UsedTradeHQ uses data only for the feature that needs it: operating the simulator, authenticating optional accounts, showing profile/community features, preventing abuse, responding to messages, delivering a voluntarily confirmed TradeHQ Newsletter subscription, diagnosing problems and improving the service.Amplitude is used for limited, explicitly triggered Arena and leaderboard-to-new-account registration analytics after renewed adult opt-in. TradeHQ measures only consenting eligible visitors and same-browser new-account confirmations within seven days; email-link confirmations in another browser and visitors who reject analytics are not included, so any conversion rate is an incomplete proxy, not a claim about all visitors. This site's Amplitude configuration disables session replay, automatic page and click capture, form interactions, network tracking and remote automatic-enablement settings. We do not claim that disabling those features makes Amplitude's pseudonymous identifiers or request metadata anonymous.Ad-serving scripts and placements are currently disabled on TradeHQ, including newly published courses, account pages and error screens. The publisher verification meta tag and ads.txt do not enable ad serving. Before advertising can be enabled, TradeHQ must verify Google site approval, suitable reviewed inventory, placement controls and applicable consent configuration. If advertising is enabled, Google and its partners may place or read cookies and use similar technologies, web beacons, IP addresses and other identifiers to deliver and measure ads. Third parties may collect information as a result of ad serving. Advertising cookies can reflect prior visits to TradeHQ or other sites and, where consent and law permit, support personalised ads. These uses remain subject to the applicable privacy choices. Advertising may be personalized, non-personalized or limited depending on consent, location and Google settings.TradeHQ does not sell simulated portfolio data to brokers or financial institutions and does not execute real-money trades.Storage, Visibility & RetentionBrowser data remains on the device until the browser, the user or TradeHQ's own reset controls remove it. Clearing all site data also removes browser-local recovery copies; download a portfolio backup to preserve it separately. Clearing browser data removes local records; it does not delete a signed-in portfolio already stored in Supabase.Optional account and community data can be stored by Supabase for as long as the related account or feature requires it. Newsletter consent records and delivery receipts are retained while relevant to operating the requested subscription, unsubscribe suppression, and compliance; contact TradeHQ to request deletion or information. New accounts start with a private profile. You may explicitly make your profile public later; only then can chosen profile fields and selected simulated statistics appear on public pages. Existing members retain their chosen visibility, and public trade-history sharing remains a separate off-by-default permission.Scored educational trophy challenges are optional for registered users. TradeHQ stores the minimal account-linked challenge ID, source version, pass/miss and score receipt, and the resulting permanent trophy ID and issue date. It does not store the answer choices you selected, your written Arena notes or a copy of each Daily case in the trophy award record. Existing device-only learning progress is not used to create server-verified public awards. Account deletion removes the separate trophy records.Trophy display is disabled by default even for a public trader profile, including older profiles that were historically public by default. After an account is confirmed and its profile is deliberately public, the owner may separately enable display of one earned trophy flair and up to three earned pinned trophies. Only the chosen trophy names/icons are shown publicly; scores, assessment dates, balances, trades, contacts and private learning history are not included. You may withdraw this permission in My Trophy Cabinet, or hide the entire profile; both actions stop the optional trophy display.The optional leaderboard attribution marker contains only a local visit timestamp and is eligible for matching for no more than seven days. If the person does not return, the expired timestamp may remain in browser storage until the next relevant page access, consent withdrawal or site-data clearing; it is then discarded or replaced. A successful attributed registration also clears the marker. Analytics and advertising data at external providers are retained according to their settings and policies; TradeHQ does not state a fixed provider retention period where it cannot verify one.TradeHQ uses hosted infrastructure and access controls intended to protect stored data, but no online service can guarantee absolute security.Age and Optional FeaturesThe core simulator works without an account. The optional account flow does not ask for age, so TradeHQ does not determine a visitor's age from that form.Public profiles and community features can publish the information and simulated statistics you choose to share. Avoid including private or sensitive information in public fields. A parent or guardian can use the contact page to raise a privacy concern involving a young user. Optional Amplitude Arena and leaderboard registration-flow analytics are unavailable unless the visitor confirms they are at least 18 and affirmatively accepts the updated permission. This declaration is not verified age assurance and does not resolve every jurisdiction's child-safety requirements. Visitors under 18 should reject analytics; the core simulator remains available.An advertising consent choice alone does not determine age or replace age-specific advertising protections where they apply.Service Providers, Cookies & Your ChoicesTradeHQ relies on third parties including Cloudflare Pages for hosting and Cloudflare Web Analytics for page-performance measurement, Google Fonts for stylesheet and font delivery, Supabase for optional authentication/database features, Resend for explicitly requested newsletter emails and contact messages, Amplitude for optional adult-consented Arena and leaderboard-to-registration analytics without session replay, and, if advertising is enabled in a future reviewed release, Google AdSense for consented advertising. These providers can process data in countries other than your own under their own legal and contractual arrangements.Optional Amplitude scripts are blocked unless a visitor expressly confirms they are at least 18 and accepts the newly expanded analytics choice. Prior v1 and v2 choices are not carried forward. Accepting stores a pseudonymous Amplitude browser identifier locally to support consented Arena measurement and the limited same-browser leaderboard registration funnel. You can reject analytics or withdraw a previous choice from this privacy page; withdrawal stops new custom events but does not automatically erase historical events already held by a provider. Contact TradeHQ for a privacy or deletion request. The Amplitude choice does not control the Cloudflare performance or Google Fonts requests described above. Analytics acceptance does not grant advertising consent.Before any future advertising release, TradeHQ must verify the applicable Google-certified consent-management configuration for regional advertising choices in the EEA, United Kingdom and Switzerland. Availability of the published message depends on Google's configuration and the visitor's region; an unavailable message does not constitute consent. The Google message lets you consent, decline or manage individual options. When it applies, use Advertising privacy choices on this page or in the footer to change or withdraw your decision.In supported US states, Google's Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information link lets you opt out of the sale or sharing of personal information for advertising. Google applies restricted data processing to applicable opt-out requests. These regional messages manage Google's advertising partners; optional Amplitude analytics are controlled separately.You can also clear browser storage/cookies, use browser privacy controls and manage ad personalization through Google Ads Settings. When the Google message is available, its partner list describes the vendors and purposes covered by your advertising choices.Depending on where you live, privacy law may give you rights to access, correct, delete, restrict or object to certain processing. Use the TradeHQ contact page for a privacy request. The exact rights available depend on your jurisdiction.Cookies and analyticsTradeHQ stores guest practice records in local browser storage. Account cash, positions and server-recorded trades are stored with Supabase. Optional analytics and advertising services can use cookies or similar identifiers after the applicable consent choice; the privacy policy explains those providers and controls.Only after a visitor confirms they are 18 or older and explicitly accepts the renewed optional analytics choice, the Practice Arena can send limited Amplitude events recording exercises viewed, started, completed or resumed, plus a same-browser day-to-day return proxy. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach.In depthThe head and shoulders pattern is a commonly described reversal formation in technical analysis. It consists of three distinct peaks: a left shoulder, a higher central peak (the head), and a right shoulder that is approximately equal in height to the left shoulder. The troughs between these peaks are connected by a line called the neckline, and a break below this neckline completes the conventional pattern description; continued decline is a hypothesis that can fail. The conventional description follows five price phases; these observations do not establish participant motives.Phase one: the market trends upward and creates the left shoulder, a normal swing high. Phase two: a pullback creates the first neckline touch. Phase three: renewed buying pushes price to a higher high (the head), recording a higher observed peak, without establishing acceleration or future direction. Phase four: another pullback returns to the neckline area, and bulls attempt one more push higher. Phase five: the rally fails to reach the head's height, forming the right shoulder — a lower peak that some analysts interpret as weakening upward momentum.The measured move technique provides a price target: measure the vertical distance from the head to the neckline, then subtract that distance from the neckline breakout point. Volume adds a separate historical observation; it does not validate a forecast. Some descriptions compare volume across the shoulders, head and neckline break. State the observation window and volume source; a lower volume does not by itself establish participants’ conviction or predict the next move. Volume alone does not establish the probability that a neckline break will persist.The inverse pattern uses three troughs rather than peaks and is commonly interpreted as a bullish hypothesis, which can fail.Key pointsThree peaks: left shoulder, head (highest), right shoulderA neckline break describes the chart; a measured target is a projection, not a guaranteed outcomeThe inverse shape can occur without a lasting upward reversalWhy it matters when you are learningDraw the three peaks and neckline, then distinguish the pattern's measured-move convention from the actual later price. A projected target is a hypothesis rather than an expected payout.Worked exercise and its limitsMark three hypothetical peaks at $50, $55 and $51 with intervening lows near $46. If you project the $9 head-to-neckline height below $46, the arithmetic target is $37. It is a projection that price need not reach.References and related pagesFidelity — technical indicators use historical observations; background, not evidence of a profitable patternDouble BottomSupport and ResistanceCandlestick PatternsPublisher and editorial approachFull glossary indexPractice deskEducational simulation only — not financial advice. The first bottom forms as the existing downtrend reaches a point where buyers emerge, creating a bounce.The subsequent rally creates the neckline — the intermediate peak between the two bottoms. However, the rally loses momentum and price declines again to retest the support level established by the first bottom. The second bottom is the critical test: if price rises again from the low, it records another bounce at that level without proving the cause or durability. In the conventional chart description, a later move above the intervening peak completes the pattern; it does not confirm a lasting reversal. A chart showing a move through such a level does not establish manipulation, the identity of a trader or actual order locations. Distinguish a suspected explanation from observable prices, actual order records and findings by a market authority; similar chart movements can have different causes. In a hypothetical example, several participants could choose exits below a recent low. If the market trades through those levels, triggered sell orders could add to selling pressure.That example describes a possible order-flow mechanism, rather than evidence that actual orders were concentrated there or that another participant deliberately moved the price. A later reversal could reflect new orders, changing liquidity, news or other causes. A wick records an interval's price range; it is not a visual signature proving a completed hunt. Public order books show displayed orders, while stop instructions, hidden orders and positions may not be publicly visible. Liquidation estimates and third-party heatmaps also require a clearly identified data source and methodology; they do not reveal every account or the location of the next price move.Charts aggregate trades over a chosen interval, so changing the interval can change how an apparent sweep looks. To examine a suspected event, first record the instrument, venue, observation time, price and volume data. Separate that record from assumptions about hidden orders or participant intent. Compare other plausible explanations and avoid treating a single chart pattern as proof. Trading safeguards involve trade-offs. A stop-market instruction can execute at a different price from its trigger, a stop-limit instruction can remain unfilled, and an unsubmitted mental exit is not an exchange order.Changing a stop level or using a time-based exit cannot guarantee protection against loss or an adverse move. TradeHQ's simulator currently supports market practice orders rather than automated stops. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach.In depthDollar Cost Averaging (DCA) is an investment strategy where a fixed dollar amount is invested into a specific asset at regular intervals — weekly, bi-weekly, or monthly — regardless of the asset's current price. Equal contributions buy more units at lower prices and fewer at higher prices. The resulting average cost can be above or below a lump-sum purchase; the price sequence and costs determine the comparison. Price variation changes the units acquired under a fixed contribution schedule; that is a purchase-timing effect rather than a guaranteed mathematical advantage.In a volatile asset like Bitcoin, a $500 monthly investment over 12 months will purchase more BTC during months when the price is depressed and less during price peaks. A fixed schedule reduces decisions about purchase dates but does not eliminate emotion, automate every product or guarantee a better result. For a hypothetical example without fees, investing $100 when a unit costs $10 buys 10 units; another $100 at $20 buys 5. The combined 15 units cost $200, or about $13.33 per unit. Investing the same $200 entirely at the first $10 price would buy 20 units, while investing it entirely at $20 would buy 10.These examples show how timing changes the quantity purchased. They do not imply that either contribution schedule will outperform across a different price path or after costs.Key pointsFixed amount invested at regular intervals regardless of priceEqual scheduled contributions buy more units at lower prices and fewer at higher prices; DCA is distinct from a discretionary decision to add to a losing positionA schedule defines purchase timing without eliminating emotion or guaranteeing a better resultWhy it matters when you are learningCalculate units bought under equal contributions at different hypothetical prices. Risk-Reward Ratio — Trading WikiLearning notes: Risk-Reward Ratio — Trading WikiThe risk-reward ratio compares a trade's planned loss with its planned gain. A 1:3 ratio means a planned $1 loss for a potential $3 gain; it does not guarantee those fills or establish a universal professional minimum.Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.Publisher and editorial transparencyPublished by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach.In depthThe risk-reward ratio (R:R or RRR) is a measurement that compares the potential loss on a trade (from entry to stop loss) against the potential gain (from entry to take profit target). Expressed as a ratio like 1:2 or 1:3, it quantifies the trade's payoff structure before entry, describing a hypothetical payoff structure, not determining whether a real transaction is suitable. A 1:2 risk-reward ratio means that for every dollar risked, two dollars of profit are targeted. A 1:3 ratio means three dollars of potential profit for each dollar of risk.A planned ratio describes selected entry and exit assumptions. A break-even calculation requires realised payoff sizes and costs; the planned ratio alone does not determine profitability. For fixed realised payoffs before costs, a 1:1 ratio breaks even at 50% wins; profitability requires more than 50%. Planned exits do not ensure those realised payoffs. With fixed realized +2R/−1R before costs, the exact break-even rate is one third; profitability requires a higher rate. At 1:3 with fixed realised gains and losses, a win rate above 25% is required before costs; exactly 25% breaks even.Under stated fixed-payoff assumptions, expected value combines the frequency and size of gains and losses. Costs and dependence also matter, and an estimate from one historical sample does not establish a future positive expectancy. A chosen planned payoff ratio is not a universal fund rule or evidence of positive realised expectancy. Use the same monetary units for the two assumed outcomes and state the convention. A hypothetical $5 loss and $15 gain give risk:reward of 1:3; gain divided by loss is instead the reward-to-risk multiple of 3. Neither describes an assured outcome.Key pointsCompares potential loss (stop loss) to potential gain (take profit)With fixed realized +3R/−1R before costs, 25% wins breaks even; profitability requires moreA planned ratio is not a universal professional minimum or evidence of positive expectancyWhy it matters when you are learningCalculate the planned ratio, then compare it with realised gains, losses and costs. A favorable planned ratio is not proof that the outcomes will match it.Worked exercise and its limitsWith fixed realized wins of +$3 and losses of −$1, a 25% win rate gives 0.25×3 − 0.75×1 = zero before costs. Adding any positive cost makes that result negative. Planned stops and targets do not establish realized amounts or win probabilities.References and related pagesSEC Investor.gov — market, limit and stop order mechanicsStop Loss HuntingLeverage TradingDrawdownPublisher and editorial approachFull glossary indexPractice deskEducational simulation only — not financial advice. Pattern forecasts and trading outcomes have not been independently validated.Understanding the Basics of Stock ChartsA stock chart is a visual representation of a security's price movement over time. The x-axis shows time (minutes, hours, days, or years) and the y-axis shows price. The most common chart types are line charts, bar charts, and candlestick charts. Candlesticks display four key observations: opening, high, low and closing prices.Each candlestick represents a specific time period. Many chart themes use green for a close above the open and red for a close below it. Colours and hollow-candle conventions vary; use the chart legend and the actual open and close values. The body of the candle shows the open-to-close range, while the thin lines above and below (called wicks or shadows) show the high and low.Candlestick names such as Doji, Hammer and Engulfing describe shapes in an observed price series. They do not prove that a reversal or continuation will occur. On TradeHQ, inspect whether the chart uses provider candles or generated practice candles before interpreting the displayed shape.Support, Resistance, and Trend LinesSupport and resistance describe areas where a price has previously paused or changed direction. They are approximate chart observations rather than floors or ceilings. A price may cross a marked level and keep moving, so compare both continuation and reversal scenarios in a journal.Trend lines connect selected price points, such as higher lows or lower highs. Their placement depends on the observation period and chosen points. A break changes that chart description; it does not establish that a new trend will continue.Volume counts shares, contracts or units traded during a stated period. A price move with high volume is an observation to investigate, not proof of reliability or institutional intent. Compare the source, interval and alternative explanations before making a simulated assumption.Key Technical Indicators for BeginnersMoving averages smooth a specified historical price series. A 50-period average crossing above a 200-period average is commonly called a golden cross; the reverse is a death cross. These lagging descriptions can change repeatedly and do not guarantee useful entry or exit timing.The Relative Strength Index (RSI) measures momentum on a scale of 0 to 100. Under common RSI settings, values above 70 are often labelled overbought and below 30 oversold. Those conventional labels are descriptions, not evidence that a reversal is imminent or certain. MACD (Moving Average Convergence Divergence) is another momentum indicator that shows the relationship between two moving averages.Practice reading charts on TradeHQ by opening any asset page — for example, NVIDIA (NVDA) or Ethereum (ETH).
