Hypothetical BTC prices are illustrative, not a verified market quotation.What Is a Market Order?A market order seeks execution at available prices rather than specifying a limit price. Execution and the final price depend on available liquidity, trading halts and other conditions. The displayed quote is not a guaranteed fill, particularly when prices move quickly.Market orders prioritize seeking execution over a specified price limit. That trade-off can involve substantial uncertainty in the eventual fill. Compare hypothetical outcomes under different liquidity and gap assumptions rather than prescribe one order type for every urgent situation.Slippage is the difference between an expected price and the actual fill. Its size varies with order size, liquidity and timing; it is not always pennies in a named asset. TradeHQ uses simplified practice market fills and does not reproduce every exchange execution condition.What Is a Limit Order?A limit order specifies the highest acceptable price for a buy or the lowest acceptable price for a sale; an execution may occur at a better price. A buy limit order executes only at your specified price or lower; a sell limit order executes only at your specified price or higher. Unlike market orders, limit orders give you price control but don't guarantee execution.In a hypothetical example, suppose Bitcoin is quoted at $68,000 while a buy limit is set at $65,000. If the market reaches that level, the order becomes eligible to fill, subject to available liquidity and order priority. A limit instruction can also be cancelled or expire before the quoted price reaches its boundary; its lifetime depends on the specified conditions.Limit orders can be useful when price control matters more than immediate execution. They are commonly used for planned entries and exits, but the trade-off is that the order may not fill at all, or may fill only partially, if there is not enough matching liquidity.When to Use Each Order TypeA market order and a limit order make different trade-offs between seeking execution and controlling price. For a learning exercise, compare possible fills during a liquid session, a wide spread and a price gap. Neither urgency nor a familiar ticker guarantees a small execution cost.A limit order specifies a maximum buy price or minimum sell price. Price control does not guarantee any fill or a full fill, even when a chart touches the level. RSI, MACD and moving-average definitions compared with the linked Fidelity guides; no predictive-performance or professional review claimed.Moving Averages: The Foundation of Trend AnalysisMoving averages smooth a selected price series rather than establish a hidden or future trend. Two commonly used calculations are the simple moving average (SMA), which weights observations in its window equally, and the exponential moving average (EMA), which gives greater weight to recent observations.A 50-period average crossing above a 200-period average is called a golden cross; the reverse is a death cross. The period might mean days or another chart interval. These lagging observations describe the selected series and do not establish that a rally or decline will follow.Shorter averages such as a 9-period or 21-period EMA react differently from longer averages. A price above an average describes its position relative to that calculation, not a guaranteed trend. TradeHQ chart controls include moving-average and volume overlays; indicator examples should match the actual chart features.RSI: Measuring Momentum and Overbought/Oversold ConditionsStandard RSI, introduced by J. Welles Wilder, expresses the relationship between smoothed gains and losses on a 0–100 scale. Fourteen periods is a common default; the conventional thresholds are descriptive labels rather than evidence of misvaluation or future direction.Readings above 70 or below 30 are conventional RSI descriptions rather than instructions to sell or buy. An extreme reading can persist. Divergence means price and oscillator observations differ; it does not prove a reversal or make one signal universally most reliable.Compare hypothetical RSI settings and record what each describes before looking at later prices. A pullback to 40–50 or a bounce to 50–60 is not a universal entry rule. TradeHQ's simplified RSI-style practice value should not be mistaken for a standard RSI calculation on historical provider closes.MACD: Combining Trend and Momentum SignalsThe Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD) is a versatile indicator that shows the relationship between two exponential moving averages — typically the 12-period and 26-period EMAs. The MACD line is the difference between these two EMAs, and the signal line is a 9-period EMA of the MACD line. The histogram shows the gap between them.A positive histogram means the MACD line is above its signal line; a negative histogram means it is below. Those relationships are often called bullish and bearish respectively, but describe the selected calculations rather than the next price move. Crossovers can reverse in both trending and sideways samples; performance depends on the rules, period, costs and comparison used.Combining indicators creates another hypothesis to evaluate, rather than guaranteeing the best results. Define each calculation, interval and decision rule, then compare against a simple baseline with the same costs and sample. TradeHQ offers a virtual spot-price practice exercise only.Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.Understanding SolanaThe simulated SOL holding represents exposure to token-price changes, not ownership in Solana Labs or an entitlement to network revenue. Network transaction fees paid in SOL, token-staking mechanics and the cost of buying or selling SOL on an exchange are distinct concepts. The TradeHQ spot simulation does not perform blockchain transactions or staking.Factors to distinguish when studying the instrumentRead Solana's primary documentation to distinguish network transaction processing and fee mechanics from exchange spot trading. Usage and technology changes may matter to market participants, but they do not determine a particular SOL price or return.Compare two dated, clearly identified price observations before calculating a percentage change. Network or ecosystem news may coincide with price movements without demonstrating that it caused them.Step by stepIdentify the instrument before doing any arithmetic: SOL is the token, a SOL/USD quote is a price per token, and an exchange venue's quoted price may differ from a separate source. Record the quote currency, source and observation time.Choose a hypothetical dollar budget and SOL unit price. Divide budget by unit price to calculate units, then add the simulator's stated 0.1% virtual order fee to estimate cash required. Use amounts solely for the worksheet, not as a recommended allocation.On /trade/sol, inspect the quoted spot price and any data-status label. No order is required for this worksheet; the simulator does not support resting limit or stop orders, short positions or staking.Write two different exit-price scenarios before reading a later quote. Calculate gross profit or loss as units times the change in dollars per SOL; subtract hypothetical buy and sell transaction fees separately.Review what the exercise could and could not show: quote observation versus actual fill, changes in SOL value versus whole-portfolio return, and missing real-world exchange costs, spread, slippage and custody.Worked hypothetical accounting exampleHypothetical example, not live market data: suppose SOL is $125 and the practice order is 40 SOL. The gross purchase value is 40 × $125 = $5,000; a 0.1% virtual buy fee is $5. If the later assumed price is $130, gross marked value is 40 × $130 = $5,200 and the gross change is $200. A hypothetical sale at $130 with a further 0.1% simulator fee of $5.20 would make the round-trip result $189.80 before any costs not simulated. If SOL instead fell to $115, the holding would be worth $4,600: a $400 gross decline before fees. These are chosen numbers, not a forecast or a liquidity guarantee.Timing and liquidityDigital-asset venues may operate around the clock, but 24/7 access does not mean identical liquidity at every moment. Compare source timestamp, spreads and event conditions when studying external market data. TradeHQ's chart can be sourced differently from its quote; inspect the data labels and avoid treating a chart candle as proof that a real-world market order would fill at that exact price.Mistakes specific to this instrumentConfusing an exchange SOL price with the on-chain fee for sending a Solana transaction.Using a marked portfolio value as if it were a guaranteed executable sale price.Ignoring the second virtual fee when calculating a hypothetical round trip.Assuming network usage or a technical announcement guarantees token-price appreciation.Reviewing the worksheetRecord the hypothetical buy and sell prices, quantity, both virtual fees, source timestamps and portfolio allocation. Separate token return from total-account return and note which slippage, spread and custody costs the simulation omits. Try a lower exit-price case as well as a higher one to test the same arithmetic.RiskSOL's token price can move rapidly in either direction. Exchange liquidity, order size, spread and execution terms affect an actual fill; network reliability and token supply information do not predict the next price. In a simulator, a displayed mark and a later virtual fill may not recreate exchange execution or custody risk. Never equate a hypothetical outcome with achievable returns.If you are learning from outside the USThis example is entirely virtual and does not require a wallet, real funds or access to an exchange. Laws and access conditions vary by jurisdiction; a financial-education worksheet is not confirmation that a venue or product is available locally.Educational simulation only — not financial advice.References and related pagesSolana practice pageAll asset guidesStrategy guidesSolana — on-chain fees (distinct from an exchange trading fee)Solana — network terminologyEducational simulation only — not financial advice. ScalpingLearning notes: ScalpingA step-by-step walkthrough of Scalping with practice on the free $100,000 simulator.Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.What it isA short-horizon price and transaction-cost comparison; no fixed interval defines the concept.Scalping describes attempts to capture small changes over short intervals. Because the intended price change is small, a spread, fee or execution delay can form a large part of the result. A two-tick cost is 20% of a ten-tick gross target, but that ratio does not establish expected profit: win frequency, adverse outcomes and all costs would also be needed.Market conditions that matterLiquidity and spreads vary by venue, instrument, session and event. A small spread observed in one period is not a permanent property or a reliable profit opportunity. Compare observations over stated dates rather than assign universally favorable trading hours.Study contextA study of how spreads, fees and latency affect short-horizon calculations; not a suitability recommendation.LimitationsSimplified fills and generated candles do not reproduce order-book priority, partial fills or intraday liquidity.The stepsChoose one instrument and explicitly fictional entry, exit and cost inputs for a short-horizon worksheet.State the chart interval and whether the observations are provider history or generated practice candles.Calculate the effect of a worse fill and a wider spread before comparing gains and losses.Record all selected cases, including unfavorable ones. TradeHQ supports manual market orders; planned stops are worksheet assumptions.Worked exampleHypothetical one-BTC worksheet: buy at $95,120 and compare exits at $95,210 and $95,080. Before costs, these are a $90 gain and a $40 loss. At TradeHQ's 0.1% fee on each side, the entry fee is $95.12. Selling at $95,210 adds a $95.21 fee, turning the gross gain into a $100.33 net loss. Selling at $95,080 adds a $95.08 fee, making the net loss $230.20. The exit prices are assumptions, not resting stop or target orders; a real fill can differ.The numbers behind itFor the same one-BTC example, cash paid is $95,120 × 1.001 = $95,215.12. Net sale proceeds at $95,210 are $95,210 × 0.999 = $95,114.79, so the round-trip result is −$100.33. The fee-only break-even exit solves exit price × 0.999 = $95,215.12, or approximately $95,310.43 before any additional costs. A higher assumed win rate cannot make this selected $95,210 exit profitable after those fees. These are hypothetical prices, not a return forecast.How it failsComparing a gross target with a result after fees as if they were the same measure.Treating a generated candle as evidence of an actual order-book fill.Changing size or exit assumptions after seeing the result and combining the changed rule with the original sample.Scope and source limitationsNo universal win rate or sufficient sample size applies. Recorded hypothetical outcomes depend on the sample design, assumptions and costs.Educational simulation only — not financial advice.References and related pagesFINRA — frequent intraday trading risks and mechanicsAll strategiesGlossaryPractice deskEducational simulation only — not financial advice. A scheduled review can fit some learners’ routines, but holdings remain exposed between observations and suitability cannot be inferred from employment status. Overnight gaps are possible when information arrives between sessions; a worksheet threshold is not an execution guarantee.Market conditions that matterAn apparent trend or pullback is a description of selected past data. A later continuation and a reversal are both possible. Earnings and other announcements can introduce overnight gaps; a planned exit does not guarantee a fill at that price.Study contextA worksheet comparing multi-day observation windows and overnight exposure; no work schedule establishes suitability.LimitationsManual review leaves exposure between observations, and an intended exit can be crossed by a gap.The stepsDefine a multi-day observation window without implying that a holding period predicts a return.Record a hypothetical entry, quantity and exit assumption before examining later observations.Compare different gap sizes and exit distances, including an unfilled or worse-than-planned exit.Keep fixed, partial and trailing exit rules in separate conceptual comparisons. Day TradingLearning notes: Day TradingA step-by-step walkthrough of Day Trading with practice on the free $100,000 simulator.Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.What it isOpening and closing all positions within a single session.Day trading usually means opening and closing positions within the same trading day. If a position is fully closed, it has no later overnight exposure, but an intended close is not guaranteed during a halt, outage or loss of liquidity. A short holding period does not make a position low risk. Frequency, costs, execution and behavior all affect the outcome.Market conditions that matterRanges, spreads and traded volumes differ across sessions and events. Selecting only sessions that later looked favorable creates selection bias. A meaningful comparison records its dates, includes unfavorable cases and uses information available before each hypothetical decision.Study contextA study of same-session accounting and transaction costs, rather than a recommendation for full-time activity.LimitationsRepeated orders add costs and operational demands. Closing by a chosen time is an assumption that can fail during a halt or outage.The stepsDefine a hypothetical session window and identify the relevant venue and calendar.State an entry and exit rule in advance, using only calculations available in the chosen data source.Calculate how repeated fees and worse fills change the same gross price outcome.Record whether the hypothetical exit occurred. Do not assume an outage or trading halt permits a closing transaction.Worked exampleIn a fictional same-session dataset, compare an observed price with its volume-weighted average and with another observation later in the session. Compare positive and negative differences, then record the extra cost of repeated transactions. No indicator-based order is required.The numbers behind itHypothetical arithmetic: fixed realized 52% wins at 1.5R and 48% losses at 1R give 0.30R gross expectancy. An arbitrary 0.5% of $100,000 is $500, so expectancy is $150 per trade and $750 across five trades before costs. This is an input-based worksheet, not observed returns or a slippage estimate.How it failsAssuming a particular hour or chart pattern guarantees a favorable range.Presenting an intended stop or session loss threshold as an enforced maximum loss.Inferring a trader’s emotional state or the next outcome from the number of recent losing trades.Scope and source limitationsThere is no dependable universal win-rate range. Evaluate the method by expectancy, drawdown, costs and consistency across a larger sample.Educational simulation only — not financial advice.References and related pagesFINRA — frequent intraday trading risks and mechanicsAll strategiesGlossaryPractice deskEducational simulation only — not financial advice. Dollar-Cost Averaging (DCA)Learning notes: Dollar-Cost Averaging (DCA)A step-by-step walkthrough of Dollar-Cost Averaging (DCA) with practice on the free $100,000 simulator.Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.What it isInvesting equal amounts on a predetermined schedule rather than selecting each purchase date based on a price prediction.Dollar-cost averaging describes a recurring cash-flow rule, not a method that removes market timing risk. The schedule reduces decisions about individual purchase dates, but entry prices and the investment's ultimate value remain uncertain. It is particularly important to distinguish gradual access to savings from choosing to hold already-available cash for later purchases.Market conditions that matterIn a steadily rising example market, earlier investment of already-available cash can outperform staggered entries because more units participate in the rise. On a falling path, staggered purchases can sometimes produce a lower average entry price, but both schedules can lose money. Any comparison must use the same asset, end date, fees and funding assumptions; cherry-picked price paths are not evidence of expected performance.Study contextA classroom comparison of repeated contributions and lump-sum purchase schedules, with equal total funding and clearly stated cash-availability dates.LimitationsDCA does not prevent loss, make an unsafe investment suitable, or outperform a lump sum consistently; transaction fees can accumulate.The stepsChoose an entirely hypothetical instrument, a purchase calendar and a fixed cash contribution.At each assumed date, divide the contribution by the unit price to calculate units. If fees apply, subtract the fee from the cash available for units.Add contributions and units, then calculate average cost per unit as total purchase cost divided by units acquired; this is a historical accounting figure, not a future-value estimate.Compare the final market value against total contributions at the same end date, using a separate scenario where the full amount was available from the start.Discuss access to funds, costs, permanent-loss risk and what would happen if purchases stopped early; no schedule guarantees a profit.Worked exampleHypothetical fee-free worksheet: contribute $100 when the unit prices are $10, $8 and $12. The purchases acquire 10, 12.5 and about 8.333 units respectively, or about 30.833 units for $300. At the final $12 price they are worth approximately $370, a $70 unrealized gain before any costs. A $300 lump sum at the initial $10 price, if all funds had been available then, buys 30 units worth $360 at the end. This one invented path cannot establish which schedule performs better generally.The numbers behind itIn the fee-free three-date example, unit total = $100/$10 + $100/$8 + $100/$12 = approximately 30.8333 units. Historical average cash paid per unit = $300/30.8333 = approximately $9.73. At a final quoted $12, marked value ≈ $370 and gain ≈ $70. An alternative $300 lump sum at $10 acquires 30 units with marked value $360. Change the price sequence and the comparison may reverse; no realistic return estimate is implied.How it failsDescribing DCA as a guarantee of a lower average entry price or positive returns.Comparing a lump sum invested on day one with periodic savings that were not available on day one.Overlooking transaction fees, uninvested cash and the possibility of permanent impairment.Scope and source limitationsMeasure adherence to a schedule separately from returns. Outcomes depend on the path of prices, fee terms, what was purchased and when cash was actually available.Educational simulation only — not financial advice.References and related pagesU.S. SEC Investor.gov — Dollar-Cost AveragingAll strategiesGlossaryPractice deskEducational simulation only — not financial advice. Fourteen periods is a common setting; the interval must also be stated. Conventional threshold labels describe the calculation. They do not establish that an asset is mispriced or that a price reversal must follow.Market conditions that matterRSI can remain extreme during a sustained move or cross its thresholds repeatedly. Comparing samples labeled trending and ranging requires a rule for those labels that does not use future information. A second indicator shares price inputs and is not necessarily independent confirmation.Study contextStudying how the same oscillator threshold behaves in different historical samples.LimitationsAn extreme reading can persist. Neither a threshold nor a second chart pattern proves a reversal.The stepsSpecify a standard RSI calculation and interval using a source that supplies the necessary historical prices.Mark the conventional 30 and 70 thresholds as descriptions, then record all observations meeting them.Compare later continuation and reversal cases under the same sampling and cost assumptions.Treat entry and exit choices as separate hypothetical rules. Compare a later continuation and a later reversal. For a concrete comparison, label a five-bar sequence of hypothetical MACD values and identify exactly which bar produces a crossover rather than drawing a line after seeing the outcome. Record whether the signal was calculated at bar close or while the bar was still forming; that difference can alter whether a crossing appears at all. What Is an Option? Calls & Puts ExplainedLearning notes: What Is an Option? Calls & Puts ExplainedA stock option gives its buyer a contractual right; contract size, exercise style and settlement terms determine what that right involves. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice.Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.SummaryA stock option gives its buyer a contractual right; contract size, exercise style and settlement terms determine what that right involves.The core definitionThis lesson focuses on standard unadjusted US equity options, which generally cover 100 shares. A call gives its buyer a right to buy and a put a right to sell at the strike under the contract terms. American-style options can be exercised before expiry; European-style options have a different exercise schedule. Adjusted contracts and cash-settled index options can have different deliverables. The writer takes the corresponding obligation. Read the specific contract and OCC risk disclosure rather than assume every option is identical.For a standard unadjusted 100-share contract, the quoted premium is stated per share. An option premium depends on multiple pricing inputs, including the underlying price, strike, remaining time, implied volatility, interest rates and dividends. It is not a direct measure of an individual participant's expectations.Why options existA share holder can buy a put to offset some losses below its strike during the option term, at the cost of its premium. A covered call adds premium income but limits upside and retains substantial share-price risk. These examples illustrate different payoffs; neither is a guaranteed return or a universally suitable position.A simple worked exampleImagine Apple trades at $180 and you buy one 30-day $185 call for $3.00 ($300 total). Three things can happen. If Apple closes above $188 on expiration, you're profitable — the intrinsic value of the call exceeds what you paid. An expiration price strictly between $185 and $188 gives the call intrinsic value but a net loss before costs; $188 is gross break-even. If it closes at or below $185, the call expires worthless and you lose the full $300 — but nothing more. These are hypothetical expiration payoffs before costs for the purchased option alone. Exercise can create a stock position with separate funding and market risk. Short options have different obligations, and an uncovered short call can have unlimited loss.What you can practise on TradeHQTradeHQ supports spot instruments, including shares and ETFs, with $100,000 virtual capital. It does not model option strikes, expirations or premiums. Use this lesson's worked examples to calculate hypothetical contract payoffs on paper; buying an underlying share in the simulator is a different transaction from buying an option on it.> Options are contracts, not shares. Time value generally erodes as expiry approaches, but the total premium can rise or fall with other pricing inputs.(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)Key takeawaysA standard unadjusted US equity option generally covers 100 shares; adjusted and other contracts can differ.At expiration, before costs, a purchased call has a net gain above strike + premium; a purchased put has a net gain below strike − premium. Those levels are break-even prices.A purchased option held without exercise can lose its premium plus costs; exercise can create a separate underlying position and obligations.Options can be used for hedging and speculation; their risk depends on the position and contract.Check your understandingHow many shares does one standard US equity option contract control? Options: 10; 50; 100; 1,000. Correct answer: 100. Why: A standard unadjusted US equity option generally covers 100 shares. Adjusted deliverables and other option types differ.What is the maximum loss for someone who buys (goes long) a single call option? Options: Unlimited; The strike price × 100; The premium paid; The stock price × 100. Correct answer: The premium paid. Why: For the purchased option alone before exercise and costs, loss is limited to the premium. Exercise can create a separate position.A call option gives the buyer the right to: Options: Sell shares at the strike price; Buy shares at the strike price; Short the stock; Receive dividends. Correct answer: Buy shares at the strike price. Why: Call = right to buy. Put = right to sell.Buying a protective put alongside shares is an example of: Options: Eliminating every cost; A guaranteed gain; Hedging downside exposure; Avoiding contract terms. Correct answer: Hedging downside exposure. Why: A put can offset some downside below its strike, but the premium, expiry and other terms matter.SourcesOCC — Characteristics and Risks of Standardized Options (https://www.theocc.com/company-information/documents-and-archives/options-disclosure-document)OIC — Options Basics (https://www.optionseducation.org/optionsoverview/options-basics)Cboe Options Institute (https://www.cboe.com/education/)Practise this lessonUse $100,000 in virtual cash to practise supported spot instruments and general habits such as recording a trade thesis. The Greeks — Delta, Gamma, Theta & VegaLearning notes: The Greeks — Delta, Gamma, Theta & VegaThese four Greeks describe model-based sensitivities to underlying prices, time and implied volatility; they do not guarantee realized price changes. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice.Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.SummaryThese four Greeks describe model-based sensitivities to underlying prices, time and implied volatility; they do not guarantee realized price changes.Why Greeks matterGreeks are model-based sensitivities to inputs, holding other inputs fixed. Delta describes underlying-price sensitivity; gamma describes a change in delta; theta describes time sensitivity; vega describes implied-volatility sensitivity. Interest rates and dividends can also matter. Finite market moves need not equal a first-order estimate, and different pricing models can produce different values.Delta — directional exposureA delta of 0.50 per share describes an approximate $0.50 option-price change for a $1 underlying move, with other inputs held fixed. For a 100-share contract that is about $50, before gamma and other effects. Some traders use delta as a rough probability shorthand, but it is not a calibrated real-world probability and need not match the model probability of finishing in the money.Gamma — how fast delta changesGamma measures how delta changes as the underlying moves. It is often relatively large near the strike close to expiry, depending on volatility and other inputs. Dealer hedging can affect demand, but a chart or open-interest figure alone does not establish dealer positions, required hedges or the cause of a price move.Theta — the ticking clockTheta estimates an option value change as time passes under a model, holding other inputs fixed. State whether the quote is per share or per contract and whether a calendar or trading-day convention is used. Purchased options commonly have negative theta, but realised profit also depends on price, volatility and costs. Selling premium is not a guaranteed collection of that estimate.Vega — volatility sensitivityVega estimates sensitivity to a one-percentage-point change in implied volatility, with other inputs held fixed. Implied volatility can change around earnings, but it need not rise before every release or fall afterwards. A long option can lose despite a favorable underlying move if time decay and a volatility decline offset that move.> Options have several model sensitivities: delta describes underlying-price sensitivity, gamma describes how delta changes with the underlying price, and theta and vega describe time and volatility sensitivities. Hold other model inputs fixed when interpreting each measure.(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)Key takeawaysDelta estimates underlying-price sensitivity, not a guaranteed payoff or real-world event probability.Gamma is often relatively large near the strike close to expiration; volatility and other model inputs also matter.Theta is a model sensitivity; other price changes can offset or exceed it.Vega measures volatility sensitivity; a change in implied volatility is a different quantity.Check your understandingWhat does theta measure? Options: Directional exposure; Time decay per day; Volatility sensitivity; Interest-rate risk. Correct answer: Time decay per day. Why: Theta is a model estimate of time sensitivity with other inputs held fixed; units and time conventions must be stated.In the lesson example, a 0.50 delta and a $1 underlying rise imply approximately what change per option share, before other effects? Options: $0.10; $0.30; $0.50; $0.90. Correct answer: $0.50. Why: 0.50 × $1 = $0.50 per share, holding other inputs fixed; this is not an event probability.Which event can be followed by a sharp decline in implied volatility? Options: A fixed time every morning; An earnings announcement resolving uncertainty; Every market opening without exception; Every dividend payment without exception. Correct answer: An earnings announcement resolving uncertainty. Why: A sharp post-announcement decline in implied volatility is sometimes called IV crush. It is not confined to earnings and is not inevitable after an announcement.Which Greek measures the rate of change of delta? Options: Vega; Theta; Gamma; Rho. Correct answer: Gamma. Why: Gamma tells you how quickly delta itself changes.SourcesOIC — Delta (https://www.optionseducation.org/advancedconcepts/delta)OIC — Theta (https://www.optionseducation.org/advancedconcepts/theta)OIC — Vega (https://www.optionseducation.org/advancedconcepts/vega)Cboe — The Greeks (https://www.cboe.com/education/tools/)Practise this lessonUse $100,000 in virtual cash to practise supported spot instruments and general habits such as recording a trade thesis. Defined-Risk Spreads — Verticals & Iron CondorsLearning notes: Defined-Risk Spreads — Verticals & Iron CondorsVertical spreads and iron condors illustrate bounded expiration payoffs, with execution and assignment risks to consider. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice.Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.SummaryVertical spreads and iron condors illustrate bounded expiration payoffs, with execution and assignment risks to consider.Comparing expiration payoffsA spread combines long and short options. Certain vertical spreads have bounded theoretical payoffs at expiration, unlike an uncovered short call. That comparison does not make spreads universally safe or suitable for beginners. TradeHQ does not execute options spreads; the examples below are worksheet exercises.Bull call spread — a hypothetical exampleAssume one standard 100-share contract per leg, the same expiration, a $180 long call costing $4 per share and a $185 short call receiving $2. The net debit is $200. With both legs resolved as the expiration payoff assumes, the maximum loss is $200 and the maximum gain is ($185 - $180) × 100 - $200 = $300, before costs. At a $182 expiration price, the $200 intrinsic value offsets the debit for gross break-even. These selected quotes are arithmetic inputs, not current Apple prices or a recommended trade.Iron condor — another payoff structureA short iron condor combines a put credit spread below and a call credit spread above the underlying price. With all four legs intact, its expiration payoff has a maximum gain equal to the net credit when the price lies between the short strikes. Movement beyond the range can produce a loss. Time decay and implied volatility affect its value before expiration; this structure is an example for comparison rather than a preferred trade.A hypothetical sizing worksheetFor arithmetic practice, suppose a worksheet assigns 1-2% of a hypothetical $100,000 account to a trade's planned loss budget: that is $1,000-$2,000. These percentages are assumptions, not an institutional standard or a recommendation for a real account. Repeated losses reduce equity, and correlated positions can lose together. The percentage alone does not establish how many trades an account can withstand.What the payoff diagram leaves outCosts and poor fills can change realised results. American-style short options can be assigned before expiration. Exercise or assignment of only one leg can leave stock exposure, particularly near a strike at expiration. A bounded payoff diagram assumes the legs are maintained and resolved together; it is not a guarantee about every account outcome. Closing a spread can reduce remaining expiration exposure but adds execution costs and cannot undo earlier assignment.Worksheet comparisonCalculate the bull call example at expiration prices of $175, $182 and $190. Then add an assumed $8 in total costs: the gross outcomes of -$200, $0 and +$300 become -$208, -$8 and +$292. Separately describe what could happen if the short leg were assigned and the stock position remained open. Keep that exposure separate from the intact-spread payoff.(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)Key takeawaysCertain spreads have bounded theoretical expiration payoffs when their legs remain intact.The example's $200 debit and $300 maximum gain exclude costs and additional stock exposure.An iron condor's range-based payoff does not make it a preferred or safe trade.TradeHQ supports spot simulation; options spreads are studied in worksheets.Check your understandingFor the intact bull call example, maximum expiration loss before costs is: Options: Unlimited; The width of the spread; The $200 net debit; The strike price. Correct answer: The $200 net debit. Why: Both calls expire worthless below $180, leaving the $200 debit as the gross loss. Costs and separate stock exposure are excluded.An intact short iron condor has its maximum gross expiration gain when the underlying: Options: Rallies sharply beyond the upper wing; Crashes beyond the lower wing; Finishes between the short strikes; Goes to zero. Correct answer: Finishes between the short strikes. Why: The four options expire without intrinsic value between the short strikes, leaving the credit before costs.In the worksheet, 1-2% of a hypothetical $100,000 account equals: Options: $50,000; $25,000; $1,000-$2,000; $100. Correct answer: $1,000-$2,000. Why: 100,000 × 0.01 to 0.02 = $1,000-$2,000. The percentages are illustrative assumptions, not a universal standard.Why can an expiration payoff diagram understate account exposure? Options: It guarantees a profit; It includes all commissions; Assignment of one leg can leave a stock position; Spreads cannot lose. Correct answer: Assignment of one leg can leave a stock position. Why: The intact-spread payoff assumes both legs are resolved together. Assignment can create separate stock exposure and costs.SourcesOIC — Bull Call Spread and Assignment Risk (https://www.optionseducation.org/strategies/all-strategies/bull-call-spread-debit-call-spread)OIC — Short Condor (Iron Condor) (https://www.optionseducation.org/strategies/all-strategies/short-condor)OCC — Options Disclosure Document (https://www.theocc.com/company-information/documents-and-archives/options-disclosure-document)Practise this lessonUse $100,000 in virtual cash to practise supported spot instruments and general habits such as recording a trade thesis. Implied Volatility & Trading Around EarningsLearning notes: Implied Volatility & Trading Around EarningsImplied volatility is a model-implied input derived from option prices, with limits as a forecast of realised volatility. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice.Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.SummaryImplied volatility is a model-implied input derived from option prices, with limits as a forecast of realised volatility.What implied volatility actually isImplied volatility (IV) is the volatility figure that, plugged into an option pricing model, would produce the option's current market price. It is not a prediction any single person makes — it emerges from the aggregate bids and offers of every participant. Changes can reflect expected uncertainty, demand for protection and risk premiums. IV is model-dependent and need not equal later realised volatility.IV rank vs IV percentileA quoted IV value needs context before comparisons can be interpreted. IV rank commonly compares current IV with the highest and lowest observations over a specified lookback, often 52 weeks, on a 0–100 scale. A constant series has no high-low range, so the usual calculation is undefined. Under one common convention, IV percentile is the fraction of observations below the current value over a stated lookback. Check the provider's treatment of equal observations and the chosen series. Neither an IV-rank threshold nor an IV-percentile threshold establishes a buy or sell rule. Compare the chosen lookback, option expiry, price source and costs before interpreting either measure.The earnings trapImplied volatility often rises before earnings and can fall sharply afterwards. A trader can be directionally correct and still lose on a long option if the volatility drop and time decay outweigh the price move.Comparing hypothetical earnings payoffsIn a paper worksheet, compare hypothetical long-premium and defined-risk premium-selling structures around earnings to see how direction, implied volatility and the size of the actual move interact. TradeHQ does not price these structures. Avoid treating volatility selling as inherently safer; short premium can carry substantial risk.Practice loopFor a historical study, record dated option quotes and implied-volatility observations from an options-data source before and after an earnings announcement. Keep the expiry, strike and data methodology consistent, and record price changes as well as volatility changes. TradeHQ does not supply an options chain or IV-rank data. A small sample can illustrate mechanisms without establishing a reliable trading edge.(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)Key takeawaysIV is inferred from option prices under a model; it can differ from future realised volatility.IV rank contextualises today's IV against the last 12 months.IV crush after earnings can turn a correct directional bet into a loss.Elevated implied volatility changes the payoff profile of premium-selling strategies, but higher premiums also reflect higher expected uncertainty and risk.Check your understandingUnder the lesson's 52-week high-low convention, what does IV rank of 80 describe? Options: IV is at 80%; IV is toward the upper end of its observed range; IV is near a 12-month low; 80% of options are profitable. Correct answer: IV is toward the upper end of its observed range. Why: IV rank describes relative location within a specified high-low range, not the fraction of days below the current value.Why can a long option lose even if the price moves in the expected direction after earnings? Options: Because options never follow the underlying; A drop in implied volatility and time value can offset the directional gain; Because earnings cancel the contract; Because all options are illiquid. Correct answer: A drop in implied volatility and time value can offset the directional gain. Why: Option value depends on more than direction; implied volatility and time value can change sharply after earnings.What does a high IV rank tell you? Options: A premium-selling trade is guaranteed to work; Current implied volatility is high relative to its own recent range; The stock must fall; The next move will be small. Correct answer: Current implied volatility is high relative to its own recent range. Why: IV rank is context about relative option pricing, not a standalone buy or sell signal.Implied volatility is: Options: Historical vol over 30 days; An exchange forecast; The volatility that makes model = market price; The stock's beta. Correct answer: The volatility that makes model = market price. Why: IV is the vol input that reconciles a pricing model with the live option price.SourcesOIC — Vega and implied volatility sensitivity (https://www.optionseducation.org/advancedconcepts/vega)OIC — IV rank and percentile definitions (https://www.optionseducation.org/news/june-office-hours-faqs-iv-statistics-position-management-and-the-wheel-strategy)Practise this lessonUse $100,000 in virtual cash to practise supported spot instruments and general habits such as recording a trade thesis. Options Risk Management — Sizing, Rolling & Cutting LossesLearning notes: Options Risk Management — Sizing, Rolling & Cutting LossesOptions losses can be amplified by position size, leverage, volatility and time decay. This lesson measures those risks using hypothetical contract examples. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice.Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.SummaryOptions losses can be amplified by position size, leverage, volatility and time decay. This lesson measures those risks using hypothetical contract examples.Illustrative 1% budget for a defined-risk worksheetThe worksheet uses a hypothetical loss assumption for arithmetic comparison; it does not require entering any position. For example, 1% of a $100,000 practice account is $1,000. This is an educational parameter, not a universal real-money rule.Testing a hypothetical loss multiplierNaked puts and short strangles can create losses far larger than the premium collected. In a paper worksheet, model adverse moves explicitly and compare the resulting losses with a hypothetical risk budget rather than relying on one fixed multiplier. TradeHQ does not execute these option positions.Rolling — definition and limitationsRolling means closing an existing option and opening another with a different expiry and sometimes a different strike. A credit or debit alone does not determine whether the adjustment makes sense; compare the new maximum loss, break-even points, time remaining and total capital at risk in a worked example. Rolling options is not supported by TradeHQ's order engine.When to cut a lossPredefined exits can prevent open-ended decision-making, but no single percentage works for every option structure. In a worksheet with appropriate historical option prices, compare several hypothetical exit rules and record drawdown, average loss and opportunity cost. Account for execution assumptions and costs; TradeHQ's spot simulator cannot perform this options backtest.Journaling every tradeFor each hypothetical options example, record the thesis, dated volatility inputs, contract size, possible loss, exit assumptions and calculated P&L in a separate worksheet. TradeHQ's journal records supported simulator trades; it does not automatically capture options contracts or IV rank. Reviewing examples may reveal recurring mistakes, but no fixed number of trades establishes a reliable edge.(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)Key takeawaysUse a predefined practice risk budget and record the effect on drawdown.Model adverse scenarios for structures whose losses can exceed the premium collected.Evaluate a roll by its full risk profile, not only by whether it creates a credit or debit.Compare hypothetical exit assumptions in a separate worksheet; the TradeHQ spot simulator cannot backtest options.Check your understandingWhy define a risk budget before a simulated options trade? Options: To guarantee profit; To define a planned exposure or loss assumption; To predict volatility; To avoid all drawdowns. Correct answer: To define a planned exposure or loss assumption. Why: A risk budget records a planned exposure or loss assumption. It does not cap actual losses: gaps, execution, costs and contract obligations can produce a different result. No percentage fits every situation.What should be compared when evaluating a roll? Options: Only whether it creates a credit; Only the new expiry; The new risk, break-even points, cost and time remaining; Nothing — rolling is always better. Correct answer: The new risk, break-even points, cost and time remaining. Why: A roll changes several dimensions of the position, so the full risk profile matters more than credit versus debit alone.How can a hypothetical options exit rule be studied outside TradeHQ’s spot engine? Options: Assume one percentage always works; Use a separate options-data worksheet with explicit fills and costs; Change the rule after every loss; Ignore position size. Correct answer: Use a separate options-data worksheet with explicit fills and costs. Why: TradeHQ cannot execute an options backtest. A separate worksheet needs actual options observations and assumptions; a selected sample cannot validate future performance.Why journal every trade? Options: Tax only; Review recorded assumptions and mistakes; Required by regulators; Boosts win rate automatically. Correct answer: Review recorded assumptions and mistakes. Why: A journal records assumptions and observed mistakes. What Is a Futures Contract?Learning notes: What Is a Futures Contract?A futures contract is a standardised, exchange-traded agreement to buy or sell a fixed quantity of an asset at a set price on a set future date. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice.Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.SummaryA futures contract is a standardised, exchange-traded agreement to buy or sell a fixed quantity of an asset at a set price on a set future date.The core definitionA futures contract is a standardised, exchange-traded agreement with a specified underlying asset or reference, contract size and settlement date. Settlement can involve physical delivery or a cash payment under the contract rules. The clearing house acts as central counterparty to cleared trades and uses margin, settlement and default safeguards to manage risk. Clearing reduces counterparty exposure; it does not make default impossible or protect a position from market losses.Contract specifications matterEvery futures contract has a spec sheet: contract size, tick size, tick value, trading hours, delivery month, and settlement method (physical or cash). These details determine the exposure and settlement obligations. One E-mini S&P 500 contract represents $50 × the index — with the index at 5,000, a single contract has $250,000 of notional exposure.Long and short positionsA participant can open a long futures position by buying or a short position by selling the contract. A short futures position does not require first borrowing the underlying asset as a short stock sale does. Both directions remain subject to margin requirements, broker permissions and applicable exchange rules, including position limits. The contract's settlement obligations still matter; being able to sell first does not mean that trading is unrestricted.Speculators and price discoveryHedgers use futures to offset exposure to price changes in another activity or holding. Speculators accept price exposure in pursuit of a trading profit. For a hypothetical producer, a short futures position may offset some losses from a falling sale price; the hedge can be imperfect if the cash and futures prices move differently. These roles help explain why participants trade. This lesson does not assign a universal percentage of market volume to either group.(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)Key takeawaysA futures contract is a standardised exchange agreement with a specified underlying or reference and settlement terms.The clearing house manages counterparty risk through safeguards; it does not eliminate all risk.Both long and short futures positions remain subject to margin, permissions and exchange rules.Every contract has a spec sheet — always read it.Check your understandingThe central counterparty on a US futures exchange is: Options: The buyer; The seller; The exchange's clearing house; The broker. Correct answer: The exchange's clearing house. Why: The clearing house becomes the central counterparty to cleared transactions under its rules.Notional value of one E-mini S&P at index 5,000 ≈ Options: $5,000; $50,000; $250,000; $1,000,000. Correct answer: $250,000. Why: $50 × 5,000 = $250,000.Which statement about opening a short futures position is correct? Options: It removes margin requirements; It is exempt from exchange rules; It does not require borrowing the underlying asset first; It guarantees a maximum loss. Correct answer: It does not require borrowing the underlying asset first. Why: Selling a futures contract creates short exposure, subject to margin and applicable trading rules.A producer uses a short futures position to offset falling sale prices. This is an example of: Options: Guaranteed profit; Eliminating default risk; Hedging price exposure; Avoiding all settlement obligations. Correct answer: Hedging price exposure. Why: The futures position can offset some price exposure, but a hedge need not remove every risk.SourcesCME — Futures introduction and participant roles (https://www.cmegroup.com/education/courses/introduction-to-futures)CME — E-mini S&P 500 contract specifications (https://www.cmegroup.com/markets/equities/sp/e-mini-sandp500.contractSpecs.html)CME — Clearing safeguards (https://www.cmegroup.com/solutions/risk-management/financial-safeguards.html)CME — Position limits overview (https://www.cmegroup.com/education/courses/market-regulation/position-limits/position-limits-overview)Practise this lessonUse $100,000 in virtual cash to practise supported spot instruments and general habits such as recording a trade thesis. Margin & Leverage in FuturesLearning notes: Margin & Leverage in FuturesFutures margin is collateral for contract obligations. Losses and variation-margin demands can exceed an initial margin deposit. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice.Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.SummaryFutures margin is collateral for contract obligations. Losses and variation-margin demands can exceed an initial margin deposit.Margin is not what you thinkStock margin can involve borrowing to purchase shares. Futures margin is collateral, often called a performance bond, rather than a loan to purchase the contract's notional value. It does not cap losses. Exchange requirements vary by contract and market conditions, and brokers can require additional funds. The figures below are a hypothetical worksheet, not current margin requirements.Maintenance margin and margin callsMaintenance margin is the minimum account equity required to maintain a position. It is not a universal percentage of initial margin. A shortfall can require additional funds or a reduction in positions; a broker may liquidate positions under its rules. Requirements can change, and action may occur intraday. Check the contract requirements and broker agreement instead of assuming a fixed deadline or a guaranteed warning.Daily mark-to-marketFutures positions are marked to market, with gains and losses settled through variation margin. Daily settlement limits the accumulation of unpaid losses, and clearing arrangements may include intraday settlement. It does not eliminate default or overnight risk: clearing houses also use collateral and other financial safeguards. A hypothetical $2,000 loss reduces the account's funds; the timing of customer-account entries depends on the broker's arrangements.Why leverage cuts both waysFor a hypothetical E-mini S&P 500 contract at an index level of 5,000, the $50 multiplier gives $250,000 of notional exposure. A 1% index move is 50 points, or $2,500 per contract before costs. Relative to an assumed $13,000 margin deposit, that is about 19.2%; it is not a percentage of every trader's total account equity. A different index level, contract quantity or account balance changes the calculation.(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)Key takeawaysFutures margin is a performance bond, not a loan.Accounts are marked-to-market every trading day.A maintenance shortfall can require more funds, reduced positions or liquidation under broker rules.Leverage depends on contract exposure and the equity used in the calculation.Check your understandingFutures margin is best described as: Options: A loan; A performance bond; A fee; A tax. Correct answer: A performance bond. Why: It is collateral supporting the position, not a loan or a cap on losses.Futures accounts are marked-to-market: Options: Yearly; Monthly; Every trading day; Only at expiration. Correct answer: Every trading day. Why: Daily settlement moves cash in/out.In the worksheet (index 5,000, $50 multiplier), a 1% move relative to an assumed $13,000 deposit is approximately: Options: 1%; 5%; ~19%; 50%. Correct answer: ~19%. Why: $2,500 on $13,000 ≈ 19%.A margin call means: Options: You made money; A collateral shortfall may require funds or position reduction; Exchange closed; Broker owes interest. Correct answer: A collateral shortfall may require funds or position reduction. Why: The broker may require additional funds or reduce or liquidate positions under its rules.SourcesCME — Margin: Know What Is Needed (https://www.cmegroup.com/education/courses/introduction-to-futures/margin-know-what-is-needed)CME — Financial Safeguards (https://www.cmegroup.com/solutions/risk-management/financial-safeguards.html)Practise this lessonUse $100,000 in virtual cash to practise supported spot instruments and general habits such as recording a trade thesis. Contango & Backwardation — Term Structure ExplainedLearning notes: Contango & Backwardation — Term Structure ExplainedCompare prices across delivery dates and study carrying costs, supply conditions and the assumptions behind rolling exposure. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice.Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.SummaryCompare prices across delivery dates and study carrying costs, supply conditions and the assumptions behind rolling exposure.Term structure — the futures curveA futures curve compares quoted prices across the delivery dates available for a specified contract family and observation time. The number of listed expirations varies by product and exchange. Later delivery priced above nearer delivery is commonly called contango; the reverse comparison is backwardation. State which dates are being compared rather than assume the entire curve has one slope.Why contango happensCarrying costs such as storage, insurance and financing can contribute to higher prices for later delivery. A simplified example with $4 of carrying costs may illustrate that relationship, but convenience yield, constraints and market conditions also matter; there is no universal $4 premium or default curve.Why backwardation happensBackwardation means later-delivery contracts trade below nearer delivery in the comparison being made. Supply conditions and the value of immediate availability can contribute, but the curve alone does not prove a physical shortage or identify a future price direction.The roll yield trapA fund with futures exposure may replace expiring contracts according to its current published methodology. Rolling can affect performance relative to spot, alongside collateral returns, fees and the price path. A roll is not an automatic cash loss equal to the price gap; inspect the specific fund and observation period.Trading implicationsThe curve records prices for different delivery dates. It is context for an educational comparison, not an automatic top, bottom or squeeze signal and not a direct measurement of commercial hedger positioning.(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)Key takeawaysContango: later delivery trades above nearer delivery in the comparison; carrying costs can contribute.Backwardation: later delivery trades below nearer delivery; the curve alone does not establish a shortage.Futures-fund returns depend on methodology, contract price changes, collateral returns and costs.The curve shows delivery prices, not the identity or positioning of participants.Check your understandingFor two stated delivery months, what describes a lower price for the later delivery? Options: Contango; Backwardation; Equilibrium; Rollover. Correct answer: Backwardation. Why: Backwardation describes relative delivery prices; it does not by itself prove a shortage.Which factor can make a futures fund differ from spot performance? Options: Guaranteed gains; Contract selection and rolling methodology; No costs; Identical exposure. Correct answer: Contract selection and rolling methodology. Why: Methodology, contract price changes, collateral returns and costs affect fund performance.Which factor can contribute to contango in a storable-commodity example? Options: A guaranteed shortage; Carrying costs; The ticker symbol alone; A universal price rule. Correct answer: Carrying costs. Why: Carrying costs can contribute to higher deferred futures prices. Convenience yield and other conditions can offset those costs; storable commodities are not always in contango.Which condition can contribute to backwardation, without being proven by the curve alone? Options: Quiet market; Physical shortage; Delisting; Low vol. Correct answer: Physical shortage. Why: Immediate demand for physical supply and convenience yield can contribute to backwardation. The curve alone does not prove a shortage or identify participants’ motives.SourcesCME — Contango/Backwardation (https://www.cmegroup.com/education/courses/introduction-to-precious-metals/what-is-contango-and-backwardation)FRED — WTI spot-price series (not a futures curve) (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DCOILWTICO)CFTC — terminology and basis risk (https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm)Practise this lessonUse $100,000 in virtual cash to practise supported spot instruments and general habits such as recording a trade thesis. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.SummaryHedging is one use of futures. Airlines may hedge fuel, producers may hedge output, and funds may hedge equity beta.The airline case studyHypothetical cross-hedge: an airline with future jet-fuel costs considers a crude-oil futures position. Rising futures prices could offset part of a higher fuel bill, but jet fuel and crude oil are different products, the hedge quantity and delivery dates may not match, and margins can require cash before the fuel purchase. It is not a lock on the airline’s complete fuel cost.The farmer case studyHypothetical producer hedge: a farmer expecting to sell corn later takes a short futures position in a chosen contract month. A fall in the futures price could produce a gain offsetting part of a lower cash sale price. The final result also depends on local basis, quantity, crop yield, contract terms and costs. The futures entry price is not a guarantee of the final net farm receipt.Portfolio hedging with equity index futuresIn a hypothetical worksheet, $50 million divided by $250,000 of contract notional gives 200 contracts. That arithmetic assumes one-for-one exposure; actual hedge sizing also depends on portfolio beta, basis risk and contract specifications. It does not guarantee full neutralisation or establish trading volume.The hedge is never perfectBasis risk concerns changes in the relationship between the hedged exposure and the futures price. A hedge can reduce one exposure while introducing margin liquidity, execution and operational risks. Its effectiveness depends on the products, quantities, dates and outcome being measured; neither complete protection nor a fixed amount of risk reduction follows from the label hedge.(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)Key takeawaysHedging uses a position to offset a specified exposure; it need not eliminate every risk.Hedge direction depends on the specific price exposure being offset.A conceptual index-futures hedge can reduce some equity-market exposure; mismatch and other risks remain.Basis changes, cash-flow needs and mismatched quantities can affect a hedge.Check your understandingWhich conceptual futures direction offsets some exposure to a falling wheat sale price? Options: Buy wheat futures; Sell wheat futures; Buy corn futures; Buy S&P. Correct answer: Sell wheat futures. Why: A short wheat future can gain when its futures price falls, but basis, quantity and costs affect the combined result.Which conceptual crude futures position gains if its futures price rises? Options: Sell crude futures; Buy crude futures; Buy S&P; Do nothing. Correct answer: Buy crude futures. Why: The hypothetical price exposure has a positive gross change if its referenced futures price rises. Costs and the separate fuel expense still matter.Basis risk is: Options: Exchange default; Futures vs physical don't move perfectly together; Rate risk; FX risk. Correct answer: Futures vs physical don't move perfectly together. Why: Basis fluctuates.In the simplified one-for-one notional worksheet, what is the count represented by $50 million divided by $250,000? Options: 20; 200; 500; 1,000. Correct answer: 200. Reading CPI and Inflation DataLearning notes: Reading CPI and Inflation DataCPI measures selected consumer-price changes. Read the release, its definitions and components without assuming a predictable market response. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice.Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.SummaryCPI measures selected consumer-price changes. Read the release, its definitions and components without assuming a predictable market response.What CPI actually measuresThe US Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes CPI indexes measuring changes in consumer prices over time using sampled prices and expenditure weights. This lesson focuses on the all-urban-consumers index (CPI-U) and its all-items and all-items-less-food-and-energy measures, often called headline and core CPI. Core readings are used to study trends, while the FOMC states its longer-run 2% inflation goal in terms of the annual change in the PCE price index.The release mechanicsCheck the current BLS release calendar for CPI timing; scheduled releases are generally at 8:30 AM Eastern. Market reactions depend on expectations and other information. No fixed first-minute percentage move or single class of participant is established by this lesson.Consensus, surprise and market reactionA consensus figure is an aggregation of a particular survey’s forecasts, not the view of every economist. Record the provider, collection time and aggregation method before comparing it with the release. The difference is often called a surprise, but its sign alone cannot determine yields, exchange rates or share returns; expectations, revisions and other information can also matter.The three-layer readFor a study worksheet, compare the reported headline and core changes with a specifically identified expectation, then inspect the component contributions and measurement period. Headline and core answer different questions. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.SummaryYield-curve inversion has historically been associated with elevated US recession risk, but timing varies and the signal is not a standalone forecast.What the yield curve isA Treasury yield curve describes yields across maturities at a stated time. The US Treasury currently publishes daily estimated par yields for maturities from one month through thirty years. An upward-sloping curve has higher longer-term yields than shorter-term yields; a selected spread is inverted when the shorter-term yield exceeds the longer-term yield. The shape can vary over time and across maturity pairs.Why inversion can indicate recession riskAn inverted curve can reflect expectations for slower growth, lower future policy rates, or changing term premia. Historically, commonly watched Treasury-curve inversions have often preceded US recessions, but the lead time varies and the relationship is not a deterministic forecast.The 10Y-2Y vs 10Y-3MThe linked New York Fed research model uses the ten-year minus three-month Treasury yield spread to estimate recession probability twelve months ahead; the researchers explicitly distinguish these estimates from official Federal Reserve forecasts. The ten-year minus two-year spread is a different series. Model probabilities depend on the model and sample and are not certain outcomes; the two spreads need not invert on the same date.Trading around the curveThe curve is a slow-moving macro indicator. Treat it as one piece of economic context rather than as an intraday timing tool or an automatic instruction to change a portfolio.(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)Key takeawaysAn upward-sloping curve has higher longer-term yields than shorter-term yields; curve shapes can vary.Inversions have historically been associated with elevated recession risk, with timing that varies across cycles.The linked NY Fed recession model uses the ten-year minus three-month Treasury yield spread.Use the curve as one macro indicator alongside other evidence.Check your understandingInverted curve = Options: Short < long; Short > long; Flat; Negative yields. Correct answer: Short > long. Why: Short-term exceeds long-term.Which spread does the linked NY Fed recession model use? Options: 10Y-2Y; 10Y-3M; 30Y-5Y; 2Y-Fed Funds. Correct answer: 10Y-3M. Why: The linked New York Fed research model uses the 10-year minus 3-month Treasury spread; its estimates are not official Federal Reserve forecasts.What is the safest interpretation of a yield-curve inversion? Options: It guarantees a recession; It is one historical recession-risk indicator with uncertain timing; It predicts the exact market bottom; It only matters for day traders. Correct answer: It is one historical recession-risk indicator with uncertain timing. Why: Yield-curve inversion is informative context, but it is not a guaranteed or precisely timed forecast.The yield curve by itself provides: Options: An exact entry time; A dated description of yields across maturities; Guaranteed equity returns; One required asset allocation. The Dollar Index (DXY) — Reading Currency ContextLearning notes: The Dollar Index (DXY) — Reading Currency ContextDXY tracks the dollar against six currencies and offers context for studying currency exposure, with important limits. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice.Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach. No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.SummaryDXY tracks the dollar against six currencies and offers context for studying currency exposure, with important limits.What the basket measuresICE's US Dollar Index measures the dollar against six currencies: euro (57.6%), Japanese yen (13.6%), British pound (11.9%), Canadian dollar (9.1%), Swedish krona (4.2%) and Swiss franc (3.6%). It is heavily weighted toward the euro and excludes many trading partners. A DXY rise therefore does not imply the same dollar appreciation against every currency.Translation and company earningsDollar appreciation against a company's revenue currencies can reduce the dollar value of unhedged foreign earnings. The overall effect also depends on costs, hedges, pricing and the currencies involved. Federal Reserve research describes translation and export-competitiveness channels; it does not establish a universal conversion from a DXY percentage move to S&P 500 earnings per share.A currency worksheetSuppose a fictional company earns EUR 1 million and has no hedge. At $1.10 per euro, translation gives $1.10 million; at $1.00 per euro, it gives $1.00 million. That $100,000 difference is an illustration for one currency and one unchanged earnings amount. It is not an EPS forecast, and a move in DXY alone does not supply those exchange rates.Commodities and other influencesFor a dollar-priced commodity with an unchanged dollar price, a weaker local currency raises the local-currency purchase cost. In actual markets, commodity prices also change with supply, demand, inventories and interest rates. An inverse relationship with the dollar can appear in a selected sample, but it is not a fixed rule for gold or any other commodity.Dollar borrowing in emerging marketsA borrower with dollar debt and local-currency income can face a larger local-currency debt-service burden when that currency weakens against the dollar. Dollar revenues or hedges can offset some exposure. BIS research studies broader links between dollar strength and financial conditions; effects vary across economies and periods, so DXY is not an automatic equity signal.Compare indicators rather than choose oneRead DXY alongside relevant bilateral exchange rates, a broader trade-weighted dollar index, interest rates and the asset's own context. For a study exercise, compare the same dated observations over a chosen interval and report where relationships change. A correlation does not show that the dollar caused another asset's move or predict the next trade.(Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.)Key takeawaysDXY's euro weight is 57.6%; the basket does not represent every currency.Earnings effects depend on actual currency exposure, costs and hedging.Dollar and commodity relationships vary over time.Dollar debt exposure depends on the borrower's income currency and hedges.Check your understandingLargest DXY weight: Options: Yen; Pound; Euro (~57.6%); Yuan. Correct answer: Euro (~57.6%). Why: The euro has a 57.6% weight in ICE's six-currency basket.Dollar appreciation can reduce translated earnings when a company has: Options: No foreign exposure; Unhedged foreign-currency earnings; Only dollar revenue and costs; No earnings. Correct answer: Unhedged foreign-currency earnings. Why: Unchanged foreign-currency earnings translate into fewer dollars if the dollar strengthens against that currency. This is not a universal EPS forecast.A gold-DXY correlation measured over one period: Options: Guarantees the next price move; Proves dollar moves cause gold moves; May differ in another period; Is always positive. Correct answer: May differ in another period. Why: Correlation depends on the selected sample and does not establish causation or a fixed trading rule.Which borrower is directly exposed to a larger local-currency burden when its currency weakens against the dollar? Options: One with matching dollar income and debt; One with unhedged dollar debt and local-currency income; One with no debt; Every borrower equally. Correct answer: One with unhedged dollar debt and local-currency income. Why: Currency mismatch can increase the local-currency cost of dollar debt service; hedges or dollar revenues can change that exposure.SourcesICE — US Dollar Index Composition (https://www.ice.com/insights/indexation-and-etfs/managing-us-dollar-risk-in-uncertain_times)Federal Reserve — Dollar Appreciation and Corporate Profits (2015) (https://www.federalreserve.gov/econresdata/notes/ifdp-notes/2015/how-much-has-dollar-appreciation-affected-us-corporate-profits-20150717.html)BIS — Exchange Rates and Financial Conditions in EMEs (2023) (https://www.bis.org/publications/bulletin-79-lessons-recent-experiences-exchange-rates-capital-flows-and-financial-conditions-emes)FRED — Broad Trade-Weighted US Dollar Index (https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DTWEXBGS)Practise this lessonUse $100,000 in virtual cash to practise supported spot instruments and general habits such as recording a trade thesis.
